## Statement of the Wigner theorem

:::
**Theorem 33** (Wigner classification on the McGucken background). *Under Hypotheses A1--A11, every unitary irreducible representation of $\widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}^{+}(1,3)$ satisfying the spectrum condition A11 is unitarily equivalent to a representation induced via the Mackey construction from one of the following orbit + little-group representation pairs:*

| Orbit | C₁ = P^(μ)P_(μ) | Little group | Irreducible labels |
|---|---|---|---|
| Massive: p^(μ)p_(μ) =  − m²c² < 0, p⁰ > 0 |  − m²c² | SU(2) | spin $s\in\{0,\tfrac{1}{2},1,\tfrac{3}{2},\dots\}$ |
| Massless: p^(μ)p_(μ) = 0, p⁰ > 0, p^(μ) ≠ 0 | 0 | $\widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}(2)$ | helicity $h\in\{0,\pm\tfrac{1}{2},\pm 1,\dots\}$ (finite-helicity reps) |
| Zero orbit: p^(μ) = 0 | 0 | SL(2,ℂ) | trivial rep (vacuum) |

*The Casimir values (C₁,C₂) on each irreducible representation are constants by Schur's lemma; the orbit and little-group data are constants by the Mackey induced-representation construction. The tachyonic spacelike orbits p^(μ)p_(μ) > 0 and the negative-energy timelike orbits p⁰ < 0 are excluded by the spectrum condition A11.*
:::

The continuous-spin representations of $\widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}(2)$ (in which the two translation generators of the little group act non-trivially) are mathematical unitary irreducible representations of the Poincaré group but are excluded from physical particle content by the empirical absence of infinite-dimensional helicity multiplets in observed massless states. We restrict to the discrete-helicity representations, on which the two translation generators of $\widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}(2)$ act trivially and only the rotational $\widetilde{\mathrm{SO}}(2)$ contributes, yielding the helicity labels $h\in\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}$.

## Algebraic Channel: Algebraic derivation

The two Casimirs C₁ = P^(μ)P_(μ) and C₂ = W^(μ)W_(μ) of 𝔦𝔰𝔬(1,3) were established in Theorem 27(iv) and Corollary 29. By Schur's lemma, on any irreducible representation each Casimir acts as a scalar. The two scalar values (C₁,C₂) are the algebraic labels of the representation.

The translation subgroup $\mathbb{R}^{1,3}\subset\widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}^{+}(1,3)$ is abelian; by Stone's theorem (Theorem 41 of Section 8), its strongly continuous unitary representation on ℋ is generated by four mutually commuting self-adjoint operators P^(μ). The joint spectral measure of {P^(μ)} decomposes ℋ as a direct integral over momentum space:
$$\mathcal{H} \;\cong\; \int^{\oplus}_{\widehat{\mathbb{R}^{1,3}}}\mathcal{H}_{p}\,d\nu(p).$$
The spectrum condition A11 restricts the support of dν to the closed forward cone $\overline{V}^{+}$.

The Lorentz factor SL(2,ℂ) acts on $\widehat{\mathbb{R}^{1,3}}\cong\mathbb{R}^{1,3}$ via the dual of the defining four-vector representation. The orbit of a point $p\in\overline{V}^{+}$ under SL(2,ℂ) is the level set {p^(′) : p^(′μ)p_(μ)^(′) = p^(μ)p_(μ)} intersected with $\overline{V}^{+}$:
- For p^(μ)p_(μ) =  − m²c² < 0: a single mass hyperboloid H_(m)⁺ in V⁺ (massive orbit).
- For p^(μ)p_(μ) = 0, p ≠ 0, p⁰ > 0: the future null cone $\partial V^{+}\setminus\{0\}$ (massless orbit).
- For p^(μ) = 0: the singleton {0} (zero orbit).

These three orbit classes exhaust the support of dν in $\overline{V}^{+}$.

## Geometric Channel: Geometric derivation

The orbit structure has a direct geometric meaning on the McGucken background. The mass hyperboloid H_(m)⁺ is the geometric locus of four-velocities of massive particles of rest mass m, normalised by η(u,u) =  − c² along a worldline parameterised by proper time τ. The future null cone $\partial V^{+}\setminus\{0\}$ is the geometric locus of light-like four-momenta, in 1--1 correspondence with the future null generators of the McGucken Sphere Σ⁺(p) of Section 2. The zero orbit corresponds to the trivial vacuum representation.

The little group at a representative orbit point is the stabiliser of that point under the Lorentz action --- a geometric notion. For a massive timelike rest-frame representative p̃^(μ) = (mc,0), the stabiliser in SO⁺(1,3) is the spatial rotation group SO(3), and its preimage in the double cover SL(2,ℂ) is SU(2) (Section 2, Theorem 24). For a future null representative p̃^(μ) = (E/c,0,0,E/c), the stabiliser in SO⁺(1,3) is the Euclidean group ISO(2) of the transverse plane, with double-cover $\widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}(2)$ in SL(2,ℂ).

## Channel-bridge synthesis

:::
**Proposition 34** (Channel synthesis for Wigner). *The algebraic classification by Casimir values (Algebraic Channel) and the geometric classification by Lorentz orbits and little-group stabilisers (Geometric Channel) coincide. The bridge is the Mackey induced-representation construction, which maps an orbit + little-group-irrep pair to a unitary irreducible representation of the full semidirect product, and which is faithful and exhaustive in the regular case.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The Mackey machine for semidirect products G = N ⋊ H, with N a locally compact abelian normal subgroup, classifies the unitary irreducible representations of G as follows. The dual group N̂ is acted on by H; assume the action is regular (orbits are locally closed and orbit spaces are smooth in the Mackey sense). For each H-orbit 𝒪 ⊂ N̂, choose a representative χ ∈ 𝒪 with stabiliser H_(χ) ⊂ H; for each irreducible unitary representation π of H_(χ), the induced representation Ind_(N ⋊ H_(χ))^(N ⋊ H)(χ⊗π) is a unitary irreducible representation of G. Every unitary irreducible representation of G arises this way, and two such induced representations are unitarily equivalent iff the orbits coincide and the little-group representations are unitarily equivalent.

We verify the hypotheses for $G = \widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}^{+}(1,3)$:
- N = ℝ^(1, 3) is abelian and closed; its dual is $\widehat{\mathbb{R}^{1,3}}\cong\mathbb{R}^{1,3}$ (canonically, via the McGucken-generated pairing ⟨p, a⟩ = p^(μ)a_(μ)).
- H = SL(2,ℂ) is locally compact and acts on N̂ via the four-vector representation of its projection SO⁺(1,3).
- Regularity (Mackey's condition): the orbits of SO⁺(1,3) on $\overline{V}^{+}$ are the mass hyperboloids H_(m)⁺ (m > 0), the punctured forward null cone $\partial V^{+}\setminus\{0\}$, and the singleton {0}. Each is a smooth submanifold (orbits are locally closed; the orbit space is Hausdorff under the standard topology on $\overline{V}^{+}$).

Therefore Mackey's theorem applies. The Algebraic Channel's algebraic labels (C₁,C₂) are the orbit invariant (C₁ = p^(μ)p_(μ) on the orbit) and the little-group Casimir value (C₂ identifies the spin/helicity label of the little-group irrep). The Geometric Channel's geometric labels (orbit type and stabiliser) are the input to the Mackey induction. The two labellings coincide.

The shared invariant carrying the bridge is the McGucken-generated metric η: it appears in the Algebraic Channel via the Casimir formula C₁ = η_(μν)P^(μ)P^(ν) and in the Geometric Channel via the orbit equation η(p,p) =  − m²c². Both occurrences are the same form, generated by Lemma 1. ◼
:::

## Proof of Theorem 33

::: proof
*Proof of Theorem 33.* Let U be a unitary irreducible representation of $\widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}^{+}(1,3)$ on ℋ satisfying A10--A11.

*Step 1: spectral decomposition.* Restrict U to the abelian subgroup $\mathbb{R}^{1,3}\subset\widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}^{+}(1,3)$. By Stone's theorem (Theorem 41 of Section 8) the four translation generators P^(μ) are mutually commuting self-adjoint operators with joint spectral measure E(⋅) on ℝ^(1, 3). By the spectrum condition A11, $\mathrm{supp}(E)\subset\overline{V}^{+}$.

*Step 2: orbit analysis.* The Lorentz factor SL(2,ℂ) acts on the spectral measure E(⋅) by U(Λ)E(B)U(Λ)⁻¹ = E(ΛB) for any Borel set $B\subset\widehat{\mathbb{R}^{1,3}}$. Irreducibility of U forces E to be supported on a single Lorentz orbit in $\overline{V}^{+}$; this is a standard consequence of the fact that any invariant orthogonal decomposition of ℋ would reduce U.

*Step 3: classification of orbits in $\overline{V}^{+}$.* The Lorentz orbits in $\overline{V}^{+}$ are exactly:
- H_(m)⁺ = {p : p^(μ)p_(μ) =  − m²c², p⁰ > 0} for m > 0 (massive timelike orbits),
- $\partial V^{+}\setminus\{0\}$ (the future-pointing null orbit),
- {0} (the zero orbit).

The spacelike orbits {p : p^(μ)p_(μ) > 0} and the past timelike/null orbits {p : p⁰ < 0} are not contained in $\overline{V}^{+}$ and are excluded by A11.

*Step 4: Mackey induction.* By Proposition 34, U is unitarily equivalent to Ind(χ⊗π) for some orbit-representative χ (a point in the orbit) and some unitary irreducible representation π of the little group H_(χ):

- *Massive case.* Choose rest-frame representative p̃_(m) = (mc,0). Stabiliser in SL(2,ℂ) is SU(2). Irreducible unitary representations of SU(2) are labelled by spin $s\in\{0,\tfrac{1}{2},1,\dots\}$ with Casimir S² = s(s+1)ℏ². The induced representation has Casimir values C₁ =  − m²c² and C₂ =  + m²c² ⋅ s(s+1)ℏ² (sign convention as in Corollary 29).

- *Massless case.* Choose null representative p̃_(null) = (E/c,0,0,E/c). Stabiliser in SO⁺(1,3) is ISO(2); in SL(2,ℂ) it is $\widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}(2)$. Unitary irreducible representations of $\widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}(2)$ fall into two classes: (i) the continuous-spin representations, in which the two translation generators of $\widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}(2)$ act non-trivially with continuous spectrum (these are infinite-dimensional in any irreducible component and are not realised by observed particles); (ii) the finite-helicity representations, in which the translation generators act trivially and only the rotational subgroup $\widetilde{\mathrm{SO}}(2)\cong\mathbb{R}/4\pi\mathbb{Z}$ contributes, with character e^(ihθ) labelled by $h\in\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}$. We restrict to finite-helicity representations as the physically realised massless particle content. The Casimir values are C₁ = 0 and C₂ = 0 on all finite-helicity orbits, with the helicity h as an independent label.

- *Zero orbit.* χ is the trivial character of ℝ^(1, 3); the stabiliser is all of SL(2,ℂ); the only finite-dimensional unitary irrep is the trivial one (the vacuum). Irreducible *infinite-dimensional* unitary reps of SL(2,ℂ) exist (the principal and complementary series) but do not correspond to particle states.

In every case, the orbit + little-group-irrep pair determines the Casimir values (C₁,C₂) algebraically. Exhaustiveness of the Mackey list (every irreducible U arises from some such pair) gives the classification table of the theorem. ◼
:::

:::
**Corollary 35** (Tachyon exclusion from the McGucken particle spectrum). *Spacelike Wigner orbits (p^(μ)p_(μ) > 0) are excluded from the physical particle spectrum by the spectrum condition A11. Equivalently, the McGucken Principle's  + ic orientation forces the joint spectrum of {P^(μ)} into the forward light cone, and tachyonic momenta lie outside this cone.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The spectrum condition A11 restricts $\mathrm{supp}(E)\subset\overline{V}^{+}$, where $\overline{V}^{+}$ is the closed forward cone of the McGucken metric. Spacelike four-momenta p^(μ) have p^(μ)p_(μ) > 0, equivalently |p⁰| < |p|, equivalently p lies outside $\overline{V}^{+}$. Therefore tachyonic momenta are not in the support of any spectral measure satisfying A11, and the corresponding orbits are not realised by any unitary irreducible representation in the physical class.

The physical content of A11 is the positive-energy condition: in any inertial frame, P⁰ ≥ 0 as a self-adjoint operator. This is required for the existence of a stable vacuum (the lowest-energy state is bounded below) and for the relativistic stability of matter under Lorentz boosts. A spacelike orbit would have a representative p^(μ) that could be Lorentz-boosted to negative p⁰, contradicting boundedness below.

The McGucken Principle enters A11 through Hypothesis A5: the  + ic branch fixes the future temporal orientation, and the corresponding restriction of P⁰ to non-negative spectrum on the McGucken-generated future cone is the representation-theoretic transport of A5. Therefore the exclusion of tachyons follows as a consequence of the temporal orientation of the McGucken Principle, transported to the quantum representation level via Stone's theorem and the spectrum condition, rather than being an additional physical postulate. ◼
:::

### The compounded-$i$ origin of the spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ half-angle: the Geometric Channel companion to §10's Mackey induction

The Mackey induction derivation of Theorem 33 above supplies the Wigner classification algebraically: orbits of $P^{\mu}P_{\mu}$ under the Lorentz group parametrise the mass content, and the little-group irreducible representations at each orbit parametrise the spin (for massive) or helicity (for massless) content, giving the Casimir eigenvalues $(m^{2}c^{4}, s(s+1)\hbar^{2})$ of the two Poincaré Casimirs. The present subsection supplies the Geometric Channel companion — the geometric origin of why spin is half-integer, why the discrete little-group $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ arises rather than a continuous alternative, and why the double cover $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C}) \to \mathrm{SO}^{+}(1,3)$ carries physical content rather than being a technical convenience of representation theory. All three facts descend from the compounded-$i$ mechanism of Theorem PT11 (§6.20) applied to the $x_{4}$-oriented Dirac field of §29 Proposition M43.

**The compounded-$i$ mechanism on the spatial slice.** By Theorem PT11 Part A, the factor $i$ in $dx_{4}/dt = ic$, under multiplicative compounding through the exponential map, produces uniform circular rotation from stamped quarter-turned increments. The three spatial-bivector generators $\{e_{23}, e_{31}, e_{12}\}$ of the Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$ each square to $-1$ under the McGucken-derived Lorentzian metric of Lemma 1 (§3): $e_{ij}^{2} = -e_{i}^{2} e_{j}^{2} = -(+1)(+1) = -1$ for spatial indices $i,j \in \{1,2,3\}$. The bivectors therefore function as "$i$-like" imaginary units within the spatial sector, and their exponentials $\exp(\theta\,e_{ij})$ are periodic in $\theta$ with period $2\pi$. This is the compact side of the Lorentz algebra $\mathfrak{so}(1,3)$ — the compact rotation subalgebra $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ generated by the three spatial bivectors.

**The single-sided rotation rule as the unique orientation-preserving transformation.** The $x_{4}$-oriented Dirac matter field is $\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_{4}) = \Psi_{0}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \exp(I\,k\,x_{4})$ with $I = \gamma^{0}\gamma^{1}\gamma^{2}\gamma^{3}$ the Clifford pseudoscalar and $k > 0$ (§29 Proposition M43, the matter-orientation condition (M)). The $+ic$ orientation of Hypothesis A5 selects the sign of $k$; matter is $+$-oriented in $x_{4}$, antimatter is $-$-oriented.

Under a spatial rotation of the slice, the field transforms via the *single-sided* rotation rule
$$\Psi \;\mapsto\; \exp\!\bigl((\theta/2)\,e_{P}\bigr)\,\Psi$$
where $e_{P} \in \{e_{23}, e_{31}, e_{12}\}$ is a spatial bivector and $\theta$ is the rotation angle. The rule acts by *left multiplication only* on $\Psi$, in contrast to the *double-sided* rule $\Psi \mapsto R\,\Psi\,R^{-1}$ that applies to bivector-valued fields. By [MG-Paper81, Theorem IV.3], the single-sided rule is the unique transformation preserving matter's $x_{4}$-orientation: any transformation not of single-sided form would either flip the sign of $k$ in $\exp(I\,k\,x_{4})$ (violating orientation preservation) or fail to close on $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$ (violating group closure). Single-sided action is therefore forced by the $+ic$ factor $\gamma$ of the §6.14 decomposition combined with the requirement that spatial rotations act on matter as a group.

**The half-angle and the $4\pi$-periodicity.** The single-sided rule contains the *half*-angle $\theta/2$, not the full angle $\theta$. Compute:
$$\exp\!\bigl((\pi)\,e_{12}\bigr) \;=\; \cos(\pi) + e_{12}\sin(\pi) \;=\; -1,$$
$$\exp\!\bigl((2\pi)\,e_{12}\bigr) \;=\; \cos(2\pi) + e_{12}\sin(2\pi) \;=\; +1.$$
The single-sided rotor evaluated at rotation angle $\theta = 2\pi$ (one full spatial rotation) is $\exp((2\pi/2)\,e_{12}) = \exp(\pi\,e_{12}) = -1$: a $2\pi$ rotation sends $\Psi \mapsto -\Psi$. The rotor returns to $+1$ only at $\theta = 4\pi$: $\exp((4\pi/2)\,e_{12}) = \exp(2\pi\,e_{12}) = +1$.

This is the $4\pi$-periodicity of the spinor representation of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})$, the double cover of the rotation group $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ and by extension of the full Lorentz group $\mathrm{SO}^{+}(1,3)$. The double cover is *forced* by the requirement that matter's $x_{4}$-orientation be preserved under spatial rotation. The Geometric-Channel content of the $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C}) \to \mathrm{SO}^{+}(1,3)$ double cover is therefore: matter's $+ic$ orientation must be preserved; the unique orientation-preserving spatial-rotation action is single-sided; single-sided action has half-angle; half-angle rotation closes only at $4\pi$; hence $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{C})$ rather than $\mathrm{SO}^{+}(1,3)$ acts on the matter field.

**The spin operator and its eigenvalues.** In the minimal spinor representation of $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$, the three spatial bivectors are represented by
$$e_{23} = -i\sigma_{1}, \qquad e_{31} = -i\sigma_{2}, \qquad e_{12} = -i\sigma_{3},$$
where $\sigma_{k}$ are the Pauli matrices. The spin operator is
$$\mathbf{S} \;=\; \frac{\hbar}{2}\boldsymbol{\sigma},$$
with the factor $\hbar/2$ combining the $\hbar$ of action-per-radian (Theorem PT11 Part D, G2 content from [MG-Paper81, §II.5]) with the $1/2$ of the single-sided half-angle. The eigenvalues of $S_{z} = (\hbar/2)\sigma_{3}$ are $\pm\hbar/2$; the Casimir is $\mathbf{S}^{2} = (3\hbar^{2}/4)\mathbb{1} = s(s+1)\hbar^{2}$ with $s = 1/2$. The magnitude is $|\mathbf{S}| = (\sqrt{3}/2)\hbar$; the two allowed projections are the two-valuedness of the single-sided rotor.

The multiplicity $2s + 1 = 2$ of the spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ representation is the dimension of the minimal (Weyl) spinor of the Clifford algebra of the McGucken-derived four-dimensional Lorentzian metric: $2^{4/2} = 4$ splits into two chiralities (left-handed and right-handed Weyl spinors) times two spin states (up and down). The dimension count $4 = 2 \times 2$ is downstream of the four-dimensionality of the McGucken manifold (Hypothesis A1) and the Lorentzian signature $(-,+,+,+)$ of Lemma 1 (from Theorem PT7's $i^{2} = -1$).

**Half-integer spin and integer orbital angular momentum from one mechanism.** The Wigner classification of §10 Theorem 33 has $s \in \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ for massive representations (spin) and $h \in \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}$ for massless representations (helicity), permitting both integer and half-integer values. The Geometric Channel origin of both:

- *Integer values* correspond to rotations acting on the spatial profile $\Psi_{0}(\mathbf{x})$ alone — the "orbital" content of the wave function on the spatial slice. Since $\Psi_{0}(\mathbf{x})$ is unoriented in $x_{4}$, spatial rotations act on it via the full-angle rule $\Psi_{0}(\mathbf{x}) \mapsto \Psi_{0}(R^{-1}\mathbf{x})$ with full angle $\theta$, and single-valuedness under $\theta \mapsto \theta + 2\pi$ forces integer eigenvalues of orbital angular momentum $L_{z}\Psi_{0} = m\hbar\,\Psi_{0}$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$.

- *Half-integer values* correspond to rotations acting on the $x_{4}$-oriented multivector factor $\exp(I\,k\,x_{4})$ — the "spin" content of the wave function's $x_{4}$-orientation. Since the $x_{4}$-orientation is preserved by single-sided rotation with half-angle, single-valuedness closes only at $4\pi$, forcing half-integer eigenvalues of spin angular momentum $S_{z}\Psi = s\hbar\,\Psi$ with $s \in \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}$.

The two contents — orbital and spin, integer and half-integer — descend from the *same* compounded-$i$ mechanism (Theorem PT11 Part A), applied to *different* parts of the wave function. The spatial profile carries no $x_{4}$-orientation and rotates by full angle; the $x_{4}$-oriented multivector carries the $+ic$ orientation and rotates by half angle.

**SymPy verification.** The claims $\{e_{23}, e_{31}, e_{12}\}$ close on $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with $[e_{23}, e_{31}] = 2\,e_{12}$; $e_{ij}^{2} = -1$; $\exp((\pi)\,e_{12}) = -1$; $\exp((2\pi)\,e_{12}) = +1$; $\mathbf{S} = (\hbar/2)\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ has eigenvalues $\pm\hbar/2$ on $S_{z}$ and Casimir $\mathbf{S}^{2} = (3\hbar^{2}/4)\mathbb{1}$; the identifications $e_{23} = -i\sigma_{1}$, $e_{31} = -i\sigma_{2}$, $e_{12} = -i\sigma_{3}$ — have been verified by symbolic computation as consistent identities within $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$. The verifications are computational, not axiomatic; the theorem-level content is that these identities together with the $x_{4}$-oriented Dirac field of §29 M43 and the single-sided action of [MG-Paper81, Theorem IV.3] produce the spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ half-angle structure.

**Boost non-quantization as the same-fact complement.** The three boost bivectors $\{e_{14}, e_{24}, e_{34}\}$ satisfy $e_{i4}^{2} = +1$ under the Lorentzian metric ($e_{i}^{2} = +1$ for spatial index but $e_{4}$ carries the $-c^{2}$ from $\eta$; the product $e_{i}^{2}\,e_{4}^{2}$ gives $-1$ up to normalization, and the bivector square carries an extra sign to give $+1$). Boost exponentials are hyperbolic:
$$\exp(\phi\,e_{i4}) \;=\; \cosh\phi + e_{i4}\sinh\phi,$$
non-periodic in the rapidity $\phi \in (-\infty, +\infty)$. Boost rapidity is continuous and unquantized. The same-fact statement: quantization of angular momentum and non-quantization of boost rapidity are one and the same fact — the $\pm 1$ split of Clifford bivector squares under $\eta$ — viewed through the two subgroups of $\mathrm{SO}^{+}(1,3)$. Both descend from the Lorentzian signature that $i^{2} = -1$ supplies via Theorem PT7 (§6.16).

**Conclusion of §10.7.** The Wigner classification of Theorem 33 admits a Geometric Channel derivation: half-integer spin is the $4\pi$-periodicity of single-sided compounded-$i$ rotation on $x_{4}$-oriented matter; integer orbital angular momentum is the $2\pi$-periodicity of full-angle compounded-$i$ rotation on the spatial profile; the discrete little group $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ for massive representations is the compact rotation subgroup of the Lorentz algebra whose generators (spatial bivectors of $\mathrm{Cl}(1,3)$) square to $-1$, giving quantized angular-momentum spectra. The noncompact side of the Lorentz algebra $\mathfrak{so}(1,3)$ — the boost subalgebra spanned by the mixed spatial-temporal bivectors $\{e_{14}, e_{24}, e_{34}\}$ with $e_{i4}^{2} = +1$ under $\eta$ — is continuous and unquantized in rapidity. The massless little group $\widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}(2)$ is a distinct structure: it stabilises a null momentum and contains a compact $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ rotation about the propagation direction together with two transverse translations $E_{1}, E_{2}$; in the null-frame decomposition these translations combine one transverse rotation and one transverse boost as $E_{i} = J_{i} - K_{i}$, and act nilpotently on the adjoint representation (rather than squaring to $+1$). The continuous character of $\widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}(2)$ comes from the $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ of translations; the physical finite-helicity representations are the ones on which $E_{1}, E_{2}$ act trivially, leaving only the compact $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ helicity. All four contents — quantized spin, continuous boost rapidity, discrete SU(2) massive little group, and $\widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}(2)$ massless little group — descend from Theorem PT11's compounded-$i$ mechanism combined with Theorem PT7's $i^{2} = -1$ signature and the $+ic$ orientation of Hypothesis A5. The Geometric Channel derivation is the companion of the Algebraic Channel Mackey induction of Theorem 33 above; both are equally rigorous, and the Geometric Channel exposes the compounded-$i$ mechanism that makes the algebraic classification possible.

**Conclusion of Section 5.** Wigner's classification of unitary irreducible representations of the McGucken-generated Poincaré group is a theorem of dx₄/dt = ic under Hypotheses A1--A11. The two Casimirs C₁ = P^(μ)P_(μ) and C₂ = W^(μ)W_(μ) label irreducible representations by mass and spin/helicity (Theorem 33). The Mackey induced-representation construction is the algebraic--geometric bridge (Proposition 34): orbits of P^(μ) under the Lorentz group are the geometric input, and induced representations from little-group irreps are the algebraic output. Tachyonic spacelike orbits are excluded by the spectrum condition A11 (Corollary 35), which is the representation-theoretic transport of the  + ic temporal orientation of A5. The physical particle spectrum on the McGucken background is therefore: massive irreducible representations (m,s) with m > 0 and $s\in\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$; massless finite-helicity representations (0,h) with $h\in\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}$; and the vacuum (zero orbit, trivial rep).

# U(1) Gauge Invariance as a Theorem of dx₄/dt = ic

> *"As both QM and relativity naturally emerge from the quantized expansion of x₄, both QM and relativity needed the notion of i --- representing a moving x₄ perpendicular to our three spatial dimensions (dx₄/dt = ic). The astounding simplicity of the generalization of classical physical theories, which are obtained by the use of multidimensional geometry and non-commutative algebra, respectively, rests in both cases essentially on the introduction of the conventional symbol $\sqrt{-1}$."*
> --- Niels Bohr, *Discussions with Einstein on Epistemological Problems in Atomic Physics* (1949), as quoted in McGucken FQXi d/873

The imaginary unit i in the fibre of the complex line bundle, in the local phase e^(iα), and in the substrate-expansion law dx₄/dt = ic is one and the same imaginary unit. The unification is the content of Novelty 2 of Section 1.

## Additional hypothesis for Section 6

The U(1) gauge construction requires one input beyond the Lorentzian background and the quantum-mechanical framework of Section 5.

- **Hypothesis A12 (Complex line bundle).** Charged matter is described by smooth sections of a complex line bundle L → M over the event manifold M of Hypothesis A1. The fibre L_(p) ≅ ℂ at each event carries the canonical U(1) action ψ ↦ e^(iα)ψ for α ∈ ℝ/2πℤ, with i the imaginary unit of ℂ.

The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic supplies the same imaginary unit i at the level of the differential law on the four-coordinate tangent space. The identification of the i in the line-bundle fibre with the i in the McGucken Principle is principled (both are the standard imaginary unit of ℂ) rather than causal: the McGucken Principle does not force the matter field to be complex-valued; A12 does. What the McGucken Principle does is provide a non-trivial geometric role for i at the level of the differential law of the substrate, and the Hermitian-generator convention used throughout the paper (Sections 2--5) ties the same i to the algebra of observables. This unification of "i in the substrate equation" and "i in the wavefunction phase" is the content of Novelty 2 of Section 1 of this paper.

## Statement of the U(1) gauge theorem

:::
**Theorem 36** (U(1) gauge invariance is a theorem of dx₄/dt = ic). *Under Hypotheses A1--A12, let ψ be a smooth section of the complex line bundle L → M of A12. The global U(1) phase action ψ ↦ e^(iα)ψ with constant α is a unitary symmetry of any Lagrangian ℒ(ψ,∂ψ) built from |ψ|² and η^(μν)∂_(μ)ψ̄∂_(ν)ψ. Localising α → α(x) --- i.e., promoting the phase to a smooth function on M --- forces, by minimal coupling, the introduction of a U(1) connection one-form A = A_(μ) dx^(μ) transforming as*
$$A_{\mu} \;\mapsto\; A_{\mu} - \frac{1}{q}\,\partial_{\mu}\alpha(x), \qquad \psi\mapsto e^{i\alpha(x)}\psi,$$
*where q ∈ ℝ is the U(1) charge of the section. The gauge-covariant derivative*
D_(μ) := ∂_(μ) + iqA_(μ)
*satisfies D_(μ)(e^(iα(x))ψ) = e^(iα(x))D_(μ)ψ under the joint transformation. The curvature two-form*
F := dA,   F_(μν) = ∂_(μ)A_(ν) − ∂_(ν)A_(μ)
*is gauge-invariant and satisfies the Bianchi identity dF = 0 identically. The Noether current associated to the global U(1) phase symmetry of the matter Lagrangian, contracted against the curvature, produces the dynamical Maxwell equation*
d ⋆ F = J,
*where J = J_(μ) dx^(μ) and ⋆ is the Hodge star of the McGucken-generated metric η.*
:::

## Algebraic Channel: Algebraic derivation

The global phase action ψ ↦ e^(iα)ψ on the fibre L_(p) ≅ ℂ is the action of U(1) ⊂ GL(1,ℂ) by unitary multiplication. Its infinitesimal generator on the configuration space is the operator iq ⋅ 𝟙 acting on sections, where q is the charge eigenvalue. By Hypothesis A10 (Hilbert-space representation) and the standard reduction to one-particle states, the corresponding self-adjoint operator on ℋ is q N̂, where N̂ is the charge number operator with integer spectrum.

The global U(1) symmetry of a matter Lagrangian
ℒ_(matter)(ψ,∂ψ) = η^(μν)∂_(μ)ψ̄ ∂_(ν)ψ − m²ψ̄ψ
(scalar example; the Dirac case is parallel with ψ̄γ^(μ)∂_(μ)ψ) is invariant under constant α because ψ̄ψ and ∂_(μ)ψ̄∂_(ν)ψ are individually invariant (the phase factor in ψ is cancelled by the conjugate phase in ψ̄). By Noether's theorem (Theorem 30 of Section 4), the global symmetry yields a conserved current
J^(μ) = iq(ψ̄ ∂^(μ)ψ − (∂^(μ)ψ̄)ψ),   ∂_(μ)J^(μ) = 0.
The conserved charge Q = ∫J⁰ d³x is the total electric charge.

Localising α → α(x) destroys the invariance: under ψ ↦ e^(iα(x))ψ the ordinary derivative transforms as ∂_(μ)ψ ↦ e^(iα(x))(∂_(μ)ψ+i∂_(μ)α⋅ψ), picking up an inhomogeneous term i∂_(μ)α ⋅ ψ. Covariance under the localised action requires the introduction of a connection: define D_(μ) = ∂_(μ) + iqA_(μ), and impose
D_(μ)(e^(iα(x))ψ) = e^(iα(x))D_(μ)ψ.
Direct computation:
D_(μ)(e^(iα)ψ) = e^(iα)(∂_(μ)ψ + i(∂_(μ)α)ψ + iqA_(μ)^(′)ψ),
e^(iα)D_(μ)ψ = e^(iα)(∂_(μ)ψ + iqA_(μ)ψ).
Matching gives A_(μ)^(′) = A_(μ) − q⁻¹∂_(μ)α, which is the gauge transformation rule of the theorem.

The commutator of two covariant derivatives is computed as
[D_(μ),D_(ν)]ψ = iq(∂_(μ)A_(ν)−∂_(ν)A_(μ))ψ = iqF_(μν)ψ,
identifying F_(μν) = ∂_(μ)A_(ν) − ∂_(ν)A_(μ) as the field strength. Gauge invariance of F_(μν) follows immediately: under A_(μ) ↦ A_(μ) − q⁻¹∂_(μ)α, F_(μν) ↦ F_(μν) − q⁻¹(∂_(μ)∂_(ν)α−∂_(ν)∂_(μ)α) = F_(μν) by commutativity of partial derivatives.

## Geometric Channel: Geometric derivation

Hypothesis A12 supplies a complex line bundle L → M with structure group U(1). A connection on L is a ℝ-linear map ∇ : Γ(L) → Γ(T^(*)M⊗L) satisfying the Leibniz rule ∇(fψ) = df ⋅ ψ + f∇ψ for smooth f : M → ℂ. In a local trivialisation L|_(U) ≅ U × ℂ, ∇ is represented by ∇ = d + iqA for a real one-form A ∈ Ω¹(U), the *connection one-form* in that trivialisation. A change of trivialisation by e^(iα(x)) induces the transformation A ↦ A − q⁻¹dα on the connection coefficient, which is precisely the gauge transformation of the Algebraic Channel.

The curvature of ∇ is the ℂ-valued two-form F = dA + iqA ∧ A. For an abelian connection (U(1) is abelian, so A ∧ A = 0), this reduces to F = dA, with F_(μν) = ∂_(μ)A_(ν) − ∂_(ν)A_(μ) as in the Algebraic Channel. The Bianchi identity is geometric:
dF = d(dA) = 0
follows from d² = 0 in the de Rham complex. The Bianchi identity is therefore not an additional dynamical law: it is the integrability identity for the connection.

The Hodge star  ⋆  : Ω^(k)(M) → Ω^(4 − k)(M) is defined by the McGucken-generated metric η and the orientation of M (Hypotheses A1, A3). The dual two-form  ⋆ F ∈ Ω²(M) encodes the same information as F but with electric and magnetic components exchanged in a precise Hodge-dual sense. The dynamical Maxwell equation d ⋆ F = J is a statement about the divergence of F relative to η, sourced by the matter current J. Its derivation from the variational principle is given below in the Theorem 36 proof.

## Channel-bridge synthesis

:::
**Proposition 37** (Channel synthesis for U(1)). *The Algebraic-Channel construction (local phase covariance forces a connection one-form A_(μ)) and the Geometric-Channel construction (a connection on the complex line bundle L → M has coefficient one-form A_(μ) in any trivialisation) coincide. The bridge is the identification of "local trivialisation of L" with "local frame for the U(1)-action on sections of L," and the shared invariant is the gauge-invariant curvature two-form F = dA.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* A local trivialisation L|_(U) ≅ U × ℂ is precisely the choice of a non-vanishing smooth section s : U → L, equivalently the choice of a smooth U(1)-valued local frame for the fibre. Two trivialisations are related by a smooth U(1)-valued transition function g(x) = e^(iα(x)), which on sections acts by ψ ↦ e^(iα(x))ψ --- the Algebraic-Channel localised phase. The connection coefficient A in the new trivialisation is computed by the standard formula A^(′) = g⁻¹Ag + g⁻¹dg/(iq) = A − q⁻¹dα, which is the Algebraic-Channel transformation rule.

The curvature F = dA is independent of the choice of trivialisation: under the same transition function, F^(′) = dA^(′) = dA − q⁻¹d²α = dA = F. This is the gauge-invariance of F. Both channels produce the same F, and both identify it as the gauge-invariant content of the connection.

The shared invariant is therefore the curvature two-form F, which is what physically measurable electromagnetic field strengths reduce to. The connection coefficient A_(μ) is gauge-dependent (it changes by a total derivative under gauge transformations), but F_(μν) is gauge-invariant and is the physical electromagnetic field tensor.

The McGucken Principle's role in this bridge is to supply the underlying Lorentzian metric η (Lemma 1), which is used in the Hodge star and the Lorentz-covariant form of the gauge-invariant kinetic term $-\tfrac{1}{4}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$. The fibre structure of L (Hypothesis A12) supplies the same i that appears in the McGucken Principle, but as a identification rather than as a causal derivation: the imaginary unit i of ℂ is the same in both contexts. ◼
:::

## Proof of Theorem 36

::: proof
*Proof of Theorem 36.* The Lagrangian for the gauge-invariant theory of a charged scalar (or Dirac fermion, mutatis mutandis) is
$$\mathcal{L} \;=\; \eta^{\mu\nu}(D_{\mu}\bar\psi)(D_{\nu}\psi) - m^{2}\bar\psi\psi - \tfrac{1}{4}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu},$$
with D_(μ) = ∂_(μ) + iqA_(μ) acting on ψ (and D_(μ)^(*) = ∂_(μ) − iqA_(μ) on ψ̄). Gauge invariance under the joint transformation (ψ,A_(μ)) ↦ (e^(iα(x))ψ,A_(μ)−q⁻¹∂_(μ)α) was verified in the Algebraic Channel.

*Bianchi identity.* F = dA in any trivialisation, hence dF = d²A = 0 identically by the de Rham complex on M.

*Dynamical Maxwell equation from Noether.* Apply Theorem 30 (Noether) to the global U(1) phase symmetry of the matter Lagrangian ℒ_(matter) = η^(μν)(D_(μ)ψ̄)(D_(ν)ψ) − m²ψ̄ψ. The variation is δψ = iqαψ, δψ̄ =  − iqαψ̄, δA_(μ) = 0 (treating A_(μ) as a fixed external field for the matter Noether construction). The associated Noether current is
J^(μ) = iq(ψ̄ D^(μ)ψ − (D^(μ)ψ̄)ψ),
the gauge-covariant version of the previously computed free current. This J^(μ) is gauge-invariant by construction (the D's absorb the phase factors) and satisfies ∂_(μ)J^(μ) = 0 on shell.

For the gauge field, the Euler--Lagrange equation derived from variation of A_(μ) in the full Lagrangian is
∂_(ν)F^(νμ) = J^(μ).
This is the dynamical Maxwell equation in coordinate form. In the differential-form language, using the Hodge star on (M,η), this becomes d ⋆ F =  ⋆ J, which we abbreviate as d ⋆ F = J when the Hodge dual of the current is understood. The combined system {dF = 0, d ⋆ F = J} is the full Maxwell equations on the McGucken-generated background.

*Uniqueness of the minimal coupling.* Among all ℂ-linear first-order differential operators D_(μ) : Γ(L) → Γ(T^(*)M⊗L) satisfying (a) Leibniz D_(μ)(fψ) = (∂_(μ)f)ψ + fD_(μ)ψ for smooth f : M → ℂ, (b) covariance under U(1) gauge transformations as above, and (c) reduction to ∂_(μ) in the trivial trivialisation, the operator D_(μ) = ∂_(μ) + iqA_(μ) is the unique solution up to gauge transformation. This is the standard theorem for connections on line bundles. No tensor of lower differential order (i.e., a U(1)-equivariant zero-order operator) is available because the only U(1)-equivariant zero-order operator on L is scalar multiplication, which is already absorbed in ∂_(μ). Therefore A_(μ) is forced; the only freedom is its gauge orbit.

In every step, the McGucken Principle has entered through Lemma 1 (the metric η used in the Lagrangian and Hodge star) and through the identification of the i in A12 with the i in dx₄/dt = ic. No additional postulate has been inserted. ◼
:::

:::
**Lemma 38** (Uniqueness of the minimal U(1) connection). *Up to gauge transformation, the minimal-coupling covariant derivative D_(μ) = ∂_(μ) + iqA_(μ) is the unique first-order differential operator on the complex line bundle L → M that (i) is ℂ-linear in the section ψ, (ii) satisfies the Leibniz rule with respect to smooth scalar multiplication, (iii) intertwines local U(1) gauge transformations, and (iv) reduces to ∂_(μ) in the trivial trivialisation when A_(μ) = 0. Its curvature F = dA is the unique gauge-invariant local field built from A via algebraic operations and first derivatives.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The proof is contained in Theorem 36 above. Conditions (i)--(iv) determine D_(μ) up to addition of a ℂ-linear endomorphism of L commuting with U(1). The only such endomorphism is scalar multiplication; absorbing it into A_(μ) gives the displayed form.

The curvature F is the unique gauge-invariant local two-form built from A and first derivatives: any other candidate must be a linear combination of ∂_(μ)A_(ν) and A_(μ)A_(ν) with constant coefficients. For U(1) (abelian), A_(μ)A_(ν) is *not* gauge-invariant (under A_(μ) ↦ A_(μ) − q⁻¹∂_(μ)α the product A_(μ)A_(ν) picks up cross-terms involving ∂α), so the only gauge-invariant linear combination is the antisymmetric derivative ∂_(μ)A_(ν) − ∂_(ν)A_(μ) = F_(μν). Higher-order or non-local candidates are excluded by the first-order locality hypothesis. ◼
:::

**Conclusion of Section 6.** U(1) gauge invariance is a theorem of dx₄/dt = ic in the precise sense that, given (a) the McGucken-generated Lorentzian background of Lemma 1, (b) the quantum-mechanical Hilbert-space representation of A10 (itself a corpus theorem via the cogeneration cascade ℳ_(G) → 𝕄_(1, 3) → 𝒱 → ℋ, Theorem 116), and (c) the complex line bundle of A12, the localisation of the global U(1) phase invariance forces a unique connection one-form A_(μ) (Lemma 38) with gauge-invariant curvature F = dA (Theorem 36). The Bianchi identity dF = 0 is purely geometric; the dynamical Maxwell equation d ⋆ F = J follows from Noether's theorem (Section 4 --- itself a derived theorem of dx₄/dt = ic per the priority statement at Theorem 30) applied to the global U(1) phase symmetry of the matter Lagrangian, with ⋆ defined by the McGucken metric η. The factor i in the connection iqA_(μ) is the same Frobenius-forced i that appears in dx₄/dt = ic --- the Hermitian-generator convention and the McGucken-i are identified by Theorem 23 of §4.3 as the unique complex-structure generator of x₄-perpendicularity, in accordance with Frobenius's 1878 division-algebra classification. The U(1) gauge structure, the Maxwell equations, and the conserved electric current therefore all descend from dx₄/dt = ic as theorems rather than as independent postulates of the gauge-theoretic framework.

## §6′ Gauge Symmetry Is a Redundancy of Description Forced by McGucken Geometry

> *"What another put her finger on is exactly this point that when the equations have local symmetry that means that they're redundant that they're they're redundantly describing something and you would better fix the redundancy if you want to say something sensible..."*
>
> *"It's not a symmetry it's a redundancy but the redundancy is forced on us if we try to explain things."*
> --- Nima Arkani-Hamed, *Emmy Noether's Influence on Physics* (46:01--46:14, 1:09:16)

The framing of Theorem 36 above states that "U(1) gauge invariance is a theorem of dx₄/dt = ic." This phrasing is technically imprecise. By Arkani-Hamed's articulation of Noether's Second Theorem (§4′ above, Theorem 30′), local U(1) invariance is a **redundancy of description** rather than a *symmetry* in the strict sense of a transformation between distinct physical states: the field A_(μ) is over-counted, with physical states being equivalence classes [A_(μ)] = {A_(μ) + ∂_(μ)α : α ∈ C^(∞)(M)} rather than single A_(μ) configurations. The "transformation" A_(μ) → A_(μ) + ∂_(μ)α relabels the same physical state rather than connecting distinct physical states.

The precise statement of Theorem 36, recast in redundancy-language, is therefore that **the McGucken Principle forces the U(1) redundancy of description on any field-theoretic description of charged matter satisfying locality + unitarity + massless-spin-1 mediator content**. The McGucken-geometric mechanism is the absence of a globally preferred x₄-orientation phase at the spinor level; the representation-theoretic mechanism is the non-tensorial transformation of polarization vectors for massless spin-1 particles. These two mechanisms are the same fact viewed through different lenses.

:::
**Proposition 36′** (Gauge redundancy from x₄-phase indeterminacy). *The local U(1) invariance of Theorem 36 is a redundancy of description, in the sense of Noether's Second Theorem (Theorem 30′). The redundancy is forced on the field-theoretic description of charged matter coupled to massless spin-1 mediators by two equivalent mechanisms:*

*(i) Geometric mechanism (McGucken-Sphere reading): the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic supplies a globally preferred x₄-expansion direction via the  + ic orientation of A5, but does not supply a globally preferred phase reference for the x₄-orientation at the spinor level. The phase angle α(x) of a U(1)-valued spinor at each event is therefore not determined by the global  + ic alone; gauge transformations ψ ↦ e^(iα(x))ψ relabel the same physical state.*

*(ii) Representation-theoretic mechanism (Wigner-classification reading): by Theorem 33 (Wigner classification on the McGucken background), the massless single-particle representations of $\widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}^{+}(1,3)$ have stabiliser $\widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}(2)$, with the physical finite-helicity representations carrying only 2 polarizations (not 3, as in the massive spin-1 case). The Lorentz-covariant description by a four-vector A_(μ) has 4 components, exceeding the 2 physical degrees of freedom by exactly the U(1) redundancy: the polarization vector ϵ^(μ) transforms under a Lorentz boost preserving null momentum p^(μ) as ϵ^(μ) → ϵ^(μ) + α(p) p^(μ), with α(p) a Lorentz-invariant parameter. To restore Lorentz-covariance one must identify polarization vectors differing by αp^(μ) as the same physical state. In position space this becomes the gauge redundancy A_(μ)(x) ∼ A_(μ)(x) + ∂_(μ)α(x).*

*The two mechanisms (i) and (ii) are equivalent: massless particles on the McGucken background ride the McGucken Sphere Σ⁺(p) at v = c with Sphere-tangent share v_{x₄} = 0 on null worldlines (Appendix A, reading (R2); Theorem 16 of [McGuckenExperimental2026] = GR T6, Massless--Lightspeed Equivalence). Since the photon's share of the expansion vanishes, its accumulated x₄-phase functional X_{4}[γ] = ic·τ[γ] (reading (R4)) is constant along the null worldline. The absence of a global x₄-phase reference at the spinor level (mechanism i) is the geometric source of the non-tensorial polarization transformation (mechanism ii). Both reduce to the same fact: **the redundancy is forced on the field-theoretic description by the geometric fact that massless quanta carry zero Sphere-tangent share along their null worldlines on the McGucken Sphere, so no X_{4}-phase accumulates**.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* For mechanism (i), the argument is in [MG-SMGauge2026, §III.2] and is summarised at line 50 of the present paper: the  + ic orientation of A5 selects a global future-pointing direction along the x₄-axis, but the spinor representation of SL(2,ℂ) on ℂ² acquires its U(1) phase only after choice of a local frame in the spatial three-block of the McGucken Sphere; no  + ic-orientation argument fixes this phase pointwise. Localisation is therefore forced: the phase α(x) is a function of position, and the gauge-transformation freedom is the record of this pointwise indeterminacy.

For mechanism (ii), the standard Wigner argument (Weinberg I, §2.5; Arkani-Hamed talk, 1:00:00--1:09:24) proceeds as follows. The little group of a null momentum p^(μ) = (E/c,0,0,E/c) in SO⁺(1,3) is ISO(2), the Euclidean group of the plane orthogonal to p^(μ). The two-dimensional translation subgroup of ISO(2) acts on the polarization vector ϵ^(μ) at p as ϵ^(μ) → ϵ^(μ) + α₁t₁^(μ) + α₂t₂^(μ) with t₁^(μ), t₂^(μ) two null directions in the ISO(2)-translation plane, satisfying t₁ ⋅ p = t₂ ⋅ p = 0 and t₁ ⋅ t₂ = 0. Under a Lorentz transformation preserving p^(μ), ϵ^(μ) shifts by a linear combination of p^(μ) and the t_(i)^(μ). The Lorentz-covariant equivalence class containing ϵ^(μ) is therefore {ϵ^(μ) + (αp+β₁t₁+β₂t₂)^(μ)}. Imposing the physical-helicity restriction (finite-helicity representation, the two physical ISO(2)-translation parameters act trivially) leaves the residual equivalence ϵ^(μ) ∼ ϵ^(μ) + αp^(μ), which is the polarization-space form of the position-space gauge redundancy A_(μ)(x) ∼ A_(μ)(x) + ∂_(μ)α(x) via the plane-wave correspondence A_(μ)(x) = ϵ_(μ)(p)e^(ip ⋅ x/ℏ).

The equivalence of (i) and (ii): the McGucken-Sphere kinematics (Theorem 16 of [McGuckenExperimental2026]) places massless particles on null worldlines with Sphere-tangent share v_{x₄} = 0 (Appendix A, reading (R2)). Vanishing share means zero accumulated X_{4}-phase: m = 0 gives Compton coupling ω_(C) = mc²/ℏ = 0, so the Compton phase factor e^(-imc²τ/ℏ) is trivial for the photon whether one takes the rest-frame reverse-reading (unavailable, no rest frame) or the direct m = 0 substitution. There is therefore no x₄-phase reference associated to the worldline of a massless particle. This is mechanism (i). On the other hand, the absence of a phase reference forces the polarization vector to transform non-tensorially under Lorentz boosts: a boost that would acquire a x₄-phase factor for a massive particle (via ω_(C)Δτ) acquires nothing for a massless particle, so the polarization vector picks up an arbitrary p^(μ)-direction shift (the algebraic record of the missing phase). This is mechanism (ii). The two mechanisms are the same fact viewed through the geometric and representation-theoretic lenses respectively. ◼
:::

:::
**Remark 36′′** (What the McGucken framework adds beyond Arkani-Hamed's argument). *Arkani-Hamed (Lecture, 1:00:00--1:11:30) establishes that the gauge redundancy is forced on the field-theoretic description by Lorentz + unitarity + locality + the existence of massless particles with spin. His argument does not specify* which *redundancy is forced: any one of the unitary irreducible representations of $\widetilde{\mathrm{ISO}}(2)$-stabilised null orbits would force* a *redundancy structure. The McGucken framework specifies the redundancy* uniquely *as the abelian U(1) redundancy at the spinor level via the Frobenius selection of ℂ on the perpendicular x₄-axis (§4.3, [Wick34, Theorem 16] item 4): the perpendicular fourth axis carries a unique complex structure, the unique non-real Frobenius division algebra contained in ℂ, and the unique compact real form U(1) = S¹ of its automorphism group. The non-abelian extensions SU(2) × SU(3) of the Standard Model arise from internal frame indeterminacies on the McGucken-Clifford bundle ([MG-SMGauge2026, Parts I--III]) rather than from spatial-substrate indeterminacy. The combined statement is: Arkani-Hamed's argument forces* a *redundancy; the McGucken framework determines* which *redundancy is forced.*
:::

## §6′′ Aharonov--Bohm Effect as Empirical Confirmation of the Gauge Connection

> *"Classically I have a choice... you don't have to introduce A and Phi you can work with E and B. Quantum mechanically we have to if we insist on describing physics in a way that's in a manifest agreement with the principles of locality."*
> --- Nima Arkani-Hamed, *Emmy Noether's Influence on Physics* (1:00:35--1:00:54)

The derivation of the U(1) gauge connection in Theorem 36 above is a mathematical theorem: given the McGucken background and the localisation argument, the connection one-form A_(μ) is forced as a object. This raises the empirical question: does A_(μ) have direct physical significance, or is it a mathematical bookkeeping device with only the field strength F = dA corresponding to physical reality? The Aharonov--Bohm effect (Aharonov and Bohm 1959; experimentally confirmed by Chambers 1960 and Tonomura et al. 1986) settles this question empirically: A_(μ) has direct physical significance.

:::
**Proposition 36′′′** (Aharonov--Bohm as empirical confirmation of the gauge connection). *The Aharonov--Bohm effect --- the observed phase shift Δϕ = eΦ/ℏ acquired by an electron wavefunction passing on opposite sides of a magnetically-shielded solenoid carrying flux Φ, with no electromagnetic field E or B at any point along the electron path --- is the empirical confirmation that the U(1) connection one-form A_(μ) derived in Theorem 36 has direct physical significance independent of the field strength F = dA.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* In the Aharonov--Bohm setup, the electron paths γ₁ and γ₂ enclose the solenoid but do not enter the region of nonzero F. The phase difference between the two paths is the Wilson-loop integral
$$\Delta\phi \;=\; \frac{e}{\hbar}\oint_{\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}^{-1}}A_{\mu}\,dx^{\mu} \;=\; \frac{e}{\hbar}\int_{\Sigma}F \;=\; \frac{e\Phi}{\hbar},$$
where Σ is any 2-surface bounded by the loop γ₁γ₂⁻¹, and the second equality uses Stokes's theorem. The crucial point is that ∮A_(μ)dx^(μ) does not vanish even though F vanishes along the electron paths: the loop integral is the holonomy of the connection A, a global topological quantity sensitive to the flux Φ through the loop. The phase shift is experimentally observable as a shift in the electron-interference pattern in the double-slit geometry, with Δϕ proportional to Φ as predicted.

If A_(μ) were a mathematical bookkeeping device with no physical content, the phase shift would have to be expressible in terms of fields E and B along the electron paths; but E = B = 0 along those paths, so no such expression exists. The phase shift is therefore a direct empirical signature of the connection one-form A_(μ) as a physical object. The experimental confirmations (Chambers 1960 using a magnetised iron whisker; Tonomura et al. 1986 using a toroidal superconducting magnetic shield that excluded the magnetic field exactly from the electron paths via the Meissner effect) settled the question definitively.

The meaning for the McGucken framework: the connection A_(μ) derived in Theorem 36 is the physical realisation of the gauge structure forced by the geometric fact that U(1) is a redundancy of description on the McGucken background (Proposition 36′ above), rather than a derivable-from-E-and-B artifact. The Aharonov--Bohm effect is the empirical signature of this redundancy: the holonomy ∮A dx is the physical observable, and it carries gauge-invariant information about the topology of the field configuration that is not captured by the local field strength F. The McGucken framework predicts and explains this fact: massless quanta on the McGucken Sphere carry U(1)-phase information that is topologically nontrivial when integrated around closed loops, even when the local curvature vanishes along the loop. ◼
:::

# Non-Abelian SU(N) Gauge Invariance as a Theorem of dx₄/dt = ic

> *"In questions of science, the authority of thousands is not worth the humble reasoning of one individual."*
> --- Galileo Galilei

> *"We are to admit no more causes of natural things than such as are both true and sufficient to explain their appearances."*
> --- Isaac Newton, *Principia*, Rules of Reasoning

The non-Abelian extension of the U(1) gauge derivation proceeds in the same dual-channel architecture: local change of frame in an internal vector bundle, compensated by a Lie-algebra-valued connection, yields a curvature transforming by adjoint conjugation. The theorem is conditional on the empirical input of the compact gauge group G; the McGucken Principle supplies the Lorentzian base, not the choice of G.

## Additional hypotheses for Section 7

The non-abelian generalisation of Section 6 requires the following inputs.

- **Hypothesis A13 (Compact gauge group).** A compact connected real Lie group G is given, with Lie algebra 𝔤 equipped with an Ad(G)-invariant positive-definite inner product ⟨⋅, ⋅ ⟩_(𝔤) (such a product exists for compact G by averaging any inner product over the Haar measure). The typical examples relevant to the Standard Model are G = SU(N) for N = 2, 3.
- **Hypothesis A14 (Principal bundle and matter representation).** A principal G-bundle P → M over the event manifold M is given, together with a faithful unitary representation R : G → U(V) on a complex vector space V. Matter fields are smooth sections of the associated vector bundle E = P×_(R)V.

The compactness of G (A13) is what ensures the positive-definiteness of the Yang--Mills kinetic term and the unitary closure of the representation theory. The choice of G itself enters as empirical input identifying the internal symmetries of the Standard Model, rather than as a derivation from the McGucken Principle. What *is* a theorem of the McGucken Principle is the conclusion that, once such a bundle and representation are given, local gauge invariance forces a unique connection structure with curvature, in direct parallel to Section 6.

The Hermitian-generator convention is in force: choose a basis {T^(a)} of 𝔤 with tr_(R)(T^(a)T^(b)) = T_(R) δ^(ab) (Dynkin index T_(R) depending on the representation), self-adjoint T^(a) = (T^(a))^(†), and commutation relations
[T^(a), T^(b)] = if^(abc) T^(c),
with real, totally antisymmetric structure constants f^(abc). The factor i on the right-hand side is the Hermitian-generator convention used throughout the paper.

## Statement of the non-abelian gauge theorem

:::
**Theorem 39** (Non-abelian gauge invariance is a theorem of dx₄/dt = ic). *Under Hypotheses A1--A14, let ψ be a smooth section of the associated vector bundle E → M of A14, transforming in the representation R of G. The global G-symmetry ψ ↦ R(U)ψ with constant U ∈ G is a symmetry of any G-invariant Lagrangian. Localising U → U(x) forces the introduction of a 𝔤-valued connection one-form*
A = A_(μ)^(a) T^(a) dx^(μ),   A_(μ)^(a) ∈ C^(∞)(M),
*transforming under a local gauge transformation U(x) ∈ G as*
$$A_{\mu} \;\mapsto\; U A_{\mu} U^{-1} - \tfrac{i}{g}(\partial_{\mu}U)U^{-1}, \qquad \psi\mapsto R(U)\psi,$$
*where g ∈ ℝ_( > 0) is the gauge coupling. The gauge-covariant derivative*
D_(μ) := ∂_(μ) − igA_(μ)^(a) R(T^(a))
*satisfies D_(μ)(R(U)ψ) = R(U)D_(μ)ψ under the joint transformation. The curvature two-form*
F := dA − igA ∧ A,   F_(μν)^(a) = ∂_(μ)A_(ν)^(a) − ∂_(ν)A_(μ)^(a) + gf^(abc)A_(μ)^(b)A_(ν)^(c),
*transforms by adjoint conjugation F ↦ UFU⁻¹ under the gauge action. The Bianchi identity DF = 0 (with D the gauge-covariant exterior derivative) holds identically. The gauge-invariant Yang--Mills Lagrangian is*
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{YM}} \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}) \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{4}\,F_{\mu\nu}^{a}F^{a\,\mu\nu}.$$
:::

The Yang--Mills action S_(YM) = ∫ℒ_(YM) dvol_(η) is gauge-invariant (the trace pairs the adjoint transformation of F² with itself, and tr(UFU⁻¹⋅UFU⁻¹) = tr(F⋅F)), and bounded below in compact-G representations because the metric ⟨⋅, ⋅ ⟩_(𝔤) of A13 is positive-definite.

## Algebraic Channel: Algebraic derivation

The Lie algebra 𝔤 acts on V via the differential of R: a local gauge transformation U(x) = e^(iα^(a)(x)T^(a)) acts infinitesimally on ψ as
δψ(x) = iα^(a)(x) R(T^(a)) ψ(x).
The ordinary derivative fails to commute with this transformation when α^(a) depends on x:
∂_(μ)(R(U)ψ) = R(U)(∂_(μ)ψ + iR(U)⁻¹(∂_(μ)R(U))ψ) = R(U)(∂_(μ)ψ + iR(U⁻¹∂_(μ)U)ψ),
picking up a 𝔤-valued inhomogeneous term U⁻¹∂_(μ)U.

To compensate, define D_(μ) = ∂_(μ) − igA_(μ)^(a)R(T^(a)) and require
D_(μ)(R(U)ψ) = R(U)D_(μ)ψ.
Direct computation (using the cyclic identity for the 𝔤-valued one-form):
D_(μ)^(′)(R(U)ψ) = ∂_(μ)(R(U)ψ) − igR(A_(μ)^(′))R(U)ψ,
R(U)D_(μ)ψ = R(U)∂_(μ)ψ − igR(U)R(A_(μ))ψ.
Matching gives
$$R(A_{\mu}^{\prime}) \;=\; R(U)R(A_{\mu})R(U)^{-1} - \tfrac{i}{g}\partial_{\mu}R(U)\cdot R(U)^{-1}.$$
In any faithful representation this reduces to the Lie-algebra-valued transformation
$$A_{\mu}^{\prime} \;=\; UA_{\mu}U^{-1} - \tfrac{i}{g}(\partial_{\mu}U)U^{-1},$$
which is the gauge transformation rule of the theorem.

The commutator of covariant derivatives is
[D_(μ), D_(ν)]ψ =  − igF_(μν)^(a)R(T^(a))ψ,
where F_(μν)^(a) = ∂_(μ)A_(ν)^(a) − ∂_(ν)A_(μ)^(a) + gf^(abc)A_(μ)^(b)A_(ν)^(c) is the non-abelian field strength. Under a gauge transformation, [D_(μ)^(′),D_(ν)^(′)] = U[D_(μ),D_(ν)]U⁻¹, hence
F_(μν) ↦ UF_(μν)U⁻¹,
adjoint conjugation. The trace tr(F_(μν)F^(μν)) is therefore gauge-invariant.

The non-linear term gf^(abc)A_(μ)^(b)A_(ν)^(c) is forced by the non-commutativity of 𝔤: in the abelian case (f^(abc) = 0) it vanishes, recovering the U(1) result of Section 6. Its presence is the distinction between abelian and non-abelian gauge theory.

## Geometric Channel: Geometric derivation

Hypothesis A14 supplies the principal G-bundle P → M. A connection on P is a 𝔤-valued one-form ω ∈ Ω¹(P,𝔤) satisfying (i) Ad(g⁻¹)-equivariance under the right G-action, (ii) reproduction of the canonical vertical vector field under contraction with fundamental vector fields. In a local trivialisation P|_(U) ≅ U × G, the pullback of ω by a local section produces a 𝔤-valued local connection one-form A ∈ Ω¹(U,𝔤), which is the connection coefficient.

A change of local trivialisation by a smooth G-valued transition function U(x) transforms the connection coefficient by the standard formula
$$A^{\prime} \;=\; UAU^{-1} - \tfrac{i}{g}(dU)U^{-1},$$
which is identical to the Algebraic Channel's transformation rule. The curvature of ω is the 𝔤-valued two-form Ω = dω + ω ∧ ω ∈ Ω²(P,𝔤); its local trivialisation gives F = dA − igA ∧ A ∈ Ω²(U,𝔤), with the  − ig factor arising from the Hermitian-generator convention. The Bianchi identity is the geometric statement
DΩ = dΩ + [ω,Ω] = 0,
which holds identically by direct expansion using d² = 0 and the Jacobi identity for 𝔤.

The Yang--Mills action is constructed from F via the Ad-invariant inner product on 𝔤 (provided by A13) and the Hodge star on (M,η) (provided by Lemma 1):
$$S_{\mathrm{YM}} \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{2}\int_{M}\langle F,\,\star F\rangle_{\mathfrak{g}} \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{4}\int_{M}F_{\mu\nu}^{a}F^{a\,\mu\nu}\,d\mathrm{vol}_{\eta},$$
where the second equality uses the orthonormal basis {T^(a)} of 𝔤. Gauge invariance of S_(YM) follows from the Ad-invariance of the inner product, which is the content of the compactness hypothesis A13.

## Channel-bridge synthesis

:::
**Proposition 40** (Channel synthesis for non-abelian gauge). *The Algebraic-Channel construction (local G-action forces a connection one-form A_(μ)^(a)T^(a) with non-linear curvature F_(μν)^(a) = ∂_(μ)A_(ν)^(a) − ∂_(ν)A_(μ)^(a) + gf^(abc)A_(μ)^(b)A_(ν)^(c)) and the Geometric-Channel construction (a connection on the principal G-bundle P → M with 𝔤-valued curvature F = dA − igA ∧ A) coincide. The bridge is the identification of "local trivialisation of P" with "local choice of G-frame for the matter sections of E," and the shared invariant is the curvature two-form F ∈ Ω²(M,𝔤).*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* A local trivialisation P|_(U) ≅ U × G corresponds to a smooth G-valued local section of P; equivalently, to a smooth local choice of G-frame for any associated vector bundle. Two trivialisations are related by a smooth G-valued transition function U(x), which acts on matter sections as ψ ↦ R(U)ψ --- the Algebraic-Channel localised gauge transformation. The connection one-form in the new trivialisation is computed by the standard pullback formula:
$$A^{\prime} \;=\; UAU^{-1} - \tfrac{i}{g}(dU)U^{-1},$$
identical to the Algebraic-Channel transformation rule derived above.

The curvature is computed as the obstruction to integrability of the connection: F = dA − igA ∧ A, with $A\wedge A = \tfrac{1}{2}[A_{\mu},A_{\nu}]dx^{\mu}\wedge dx^{\nu}$ involving the Lie bracket. In component form, using [T^(a),T^(b)] = if^(abc)T^(c):
$$F = \tfrac{1}{2}F_{\mu\nu}^{a}T^{a}\,dx^{\mu}\wedge dx^{\nu}, \quad F_{\mu\nu}^{a} = \partial_{\mu}A_{\nu}^{a} - \partial_{\nu}A_{\mu}^{a} + gf^{abc}A_{\mu}^{b}A_{\nu}^{c}.$$
This is the Algebraic-Channel formula. The two channels produce the same curvature.

Under a gauge transformation, F ↦ UFU⁻¹ by adjoint conjugation (both channels). The trace tr(FF) is invariant, yielding the gauge-invariant Yang--Mills Lagrangian. The shared invariant carrying the bridge is therefore the curvature two-form F, viewed as the gauge-invariant content of the connection up to adjoint conjugation.

The McGucken Principle's role in this bridge is identical to its role in Section 6: it supplies the underlying Lorentzian metric η used in the Hodge star and in the $-\tfrac{1}{4}F_{\mu\nu}^{a}F^{a\mu\nu}$ kinetic term. The compact gauge group G and the matter representation R are independent inputs (A13--A14), but the *connection structure* on top of (M,η) and the *Yang--Mills dynamics* are uniquely forced by the requirement of local G-invariance, in direct parallel to the abelian case. ◼
:::

## Proof of Theorem 39

::: proof
*Proof of Theorem 39.* Each of the four claims of the theorem is verified.

*(i) The connection A_(μ)^(a)T^(a) is forced by local gauge covariance.* The argument is given in the Algebraic Channel above: the inhomogeneous term iU⁻¹∂_(μ)U in ∂_(μ)(R(U)ψ) requires compensation by a 𝔤-valued one-form A_(μ) in the covariant derivative D_(μ) = ∂_(μ) − igR(A_(μ)), with A_(μ) transforming as displayed.

*(ii) The curvature F and its component formula.* Computed as [D_(μ),D_(ν)] =  − igR(F_(μν)) in the Algebraic Channel above. The component formula F_(μν)^(a) = ∂_(μ)A_(ν)^(a) − ∂_(ν)A_(μ)^(a) + gf^(abc)A_(μ)^(b)A_(ν)^(c) follows from expanding [D_(μ),D_(ν)] using [T^(a),T^(b)] = if^(abc)T^(c) and grouping by Lie-algebra components.

*(iii) Bianchi identity.* Define the gauge-covariant exterior derivative on 𝔤-valued forms by DΦ = dΦ − ig[A,Φ], where the graded commutator on 𝔤-valued forms of degrees |α| and |β| is [α,β] := α ∧ β − (−1)^(|α||β|)β ∧ α (with ∧ combining the exterior product on forms with the matrix product after the representation R). Apply D to F = dA − igA ∧ A:
DF = dF − ig[A,F] = d(dA−igA∧A) − ig[A, dA−igA∧A].
Expand each term separately.

*Expansion of dF.* Using d² = 0 on dA and the Leibniz rule d(A∧A) = dA ∧ A − A ∧ dA (signs from |A| = 1):
dF = d(dA) − ig d(A∧A) = 0 − ig(dA ∧ A − A ∧ dA).

*Expansion of  − ig[A,F].* Distribute the bracket and use [A,dA] = A ∧ dA − dA ∧ A (since |A| = 1, |dA| = 2, sign (−1)^(|A||dA|) = (−1)² =  + 1):
 − ig[A,F] =  − ig[A,dA] − ig ⋅ (−ig) [A, A∧A] =  − ig(A ∧ dA − dA ∧ A) − g²[A, A∧A].

*Sum of the two expansions.* The four quadratic-in-A terms cancel exactly in pairs:
$$\underbrace{-ig\,dA\wedge A}_{\text{from }dF} + \underbrace{ig\,dA\wedge A}_{\text{from }-ig[A,F]} \;=\; 0, \qquad \underbrace{ig\,A\wedge dA}_{\text{from }dF} + \underbrace{-ig\,A\wedge dA}_{\text{from }-ig[A,F]} \;=\; 0.$$
The remaining cubic term is  − g²[A,A∧A]. Using $A\wedge A = \tfrac{1}{2}[A,A]$ (as a 𝔤-valued 2-form) and the graded Jacobi identity for 𝔤-valued forms applied to the triple (A,A,A) of equal degree 1:
(−1)^(1 ⋅ 1)[A,[A,A]] + (−1)^(1 ⋅ 1)[A,[A,A]] + (−1)^(1 ⋅ 1)[A,[A,A]] =  − 3 [A,[A,A]] = 0,
hence [A,[A,A]] = 0, and therefore $[A,A\wedge A] = \tfrac{1}{2}[A,[A,A]] = 0$. Collecting:
DF = 0 + 0 − g² ⋅ 0 = 0.
The Bianchi identity therefore holds identically as a consequence of d² = 0 and the Jacobi identity for 𝔤; it is a geometric identity, not a dynamical equation.

*(iv) Yang--Mills Lagrangian.* The trace tr_(R)(T^(a)T^(b)) = T_(R)δ^(ab) (with T_(R) the Dynkin index) gives, after rescaling,
$$-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}) \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{a,b}F_{\mu\nu}^{a}F^{b\mu\nu}\mathrm{tr}(T^{a}T^{b}) \;=\; -\tfrac{T_{R}}{2}F_{\mu\nu}^{a}F^{a\mu\nu}.$$
With the conventional choice $T_{R}=\tfrac{1}{2}$ (fundamental representation of SU(N), $\mathrm{tr}(T^{a}T^{b}) = \tfrac{1}{2}\delta^{ab}$), this becomes $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{YM}} = -\tfrac{1}{4}F_{\mu\nu}^{a}F^{a\mu\nu}$ as stated. Gauge invariance follows from the Ad-invariance of the trace.

In every step the McGucken Principle has entered through the Lorentzian metric η (used in the Hodge star and the index contraction in F_(μν)F^(μν)) and through Hypothesis A1 (orientation, used in defining the volume form). The gauge group G and its representation R are external inputs (A13--A14) not derived from the McGucken Principle. What is derived is the conclusion that, once G and R are given, the connection and curvature structure are forced uniquely. ◼
:::

:::
**Lemma 41** (Uniqueness of the non-abelian connection and curvature). *Up to gauge transformation, the connection A_(μ)^(a)T^(a) of Theorem 39 is the unique 𝔤-valued one-form making the covariant derivative D_(μ) = ∂_(μ) − igR(A_(μ)) intertwine the local G-gauge action. Up to multiplicative constants, the curvature F = dA − igA ∧ A is the unique gauge-covariant local two-form built from A via algebraic operations and first derivatives.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Existence of the connection is constructive (Theorem 39). For uniqueness up to gauge, suppose Ã_(μ) is another 𝔤-valued one-form with the same intertwining property: D̃_(μ)(R(U)ψ) = R(U)D̃_(μ)ψ for all U(x) ∈ G and all sections ψ. Then (Ã_(μ)−A_(μ)) is a 𝔤-valued one-form on M that is invariant under all local gauge transformations. By the faithfulness of R and the Ad-action on 𝔤, the only Ad-invariant element of 𝔤 is zero (since G is connected and the centre of 𝔤 is trivial for SU(N), N ≥ 2). Therefore Ã_(μ) = A_(μ) in a fixed gauge, and the connection is unique up to gauge transformation.

For the curvature: any gauge-covariant local two-form built from A via algebraic operations and first derivatives must be a linear combination of ∂_(μ)A_(ν)^(a) and A_(μ)^(b)A_(ν)^(c) with coefficient tensors that themselves transform appropriately under the gauge action. The unique such combination transforming by adjoint conjugation is F_(μν)^(a) = ∂_(μ)A_(ν)^(a) − ∂_(ν)A_(μ)^(a) + gf^(abc)A_(μ)^(b)A_(ν)^(c), up to an overall multiplicative constant (which is absorbed into the gauge coupling g). Higher-order or non-local candidates are excluded by the locality + first-order hypothesis.

The Bianchi identity DF = 0 holds identically (Theorem 39 proof). The dynamical Yang--Mills equation D ⋆ F = J follows from the Euler--Lagrange variation of the Yang--Mills + matter action with respect to A_(μ)^(a). This is exactly the non-abelian generalisation of the abelian case of Section 6: Bianchi from bundle geometry, dynamics from Noether applied to the matter Lagrangian's G-symmetry. ◼
:::

**Conclusion of Section 7.** Non-abelian G-gauge invariance is a theorem of dx₄/dt = ic in the same conditional sense as the abelian case: given the McGucken-generated Lorentzian background (Lemma 1) and the auxiliary inputs of a compact gauge group G (A13) and a principal G-bundle with matter representation (A14), the localisation of the global G-symmetry forces a unique 𝔤-valued connection one-form (Lemma 41) with curvature F = dA − igA ∧ A (Theorem 39). The Bianchi identity DF = 0 is geometric; the dynamical Yang--Mills equation follows from the Noether construction of Section 4 applied to the matter action. What is derived in the present chapter is the conclusion that the connection-and-curvature framework, once G is given, is unique up to gauge. The abelian case of Section 6 is recovered when f^(abc) = 0 (G = U(1)).

# Quantum-Unitary Evolution as a Theorem of dx₄/dt = ic

> *"My solution was really for the very concept of time, that is, that time is not absolutely defined but there is an inseparable connection between time and the signal [light] velocity."*
> --- Albert Einstein, *How I Created the Theory of Relativity*, Kyoto Address (1922)

> *"Should we be prepared to see some day a new structure for the foundations of physics that does away with time? Yes, because 'time' is in trouble."*
> --- John Archibald Wheeler

Stone's theorem on strongly continuous one-parameter unitary groups produces the Hamiltonian Ĥ from the time-translation subgroup of the McGucken-Poincaré group. The Schrödinger equation iℏ ∂_(t)ψ = Ĥψ is the infinitesimal form; the factor i is, once again, the same i that appears in dx₄/dt = ic.

## Hypothesis used in Section 8

We use Hypothesis A10 of Section 5 (Hilbert-space representation: a separable complex Hilbert space ℋ on which the Poincaré group acts unitarily) together with the standard Stone's theorem assumptions.

- **Hypothesis A10^(′) (Strong continuity of time evolution).** The one-parameter family of unitary operators {U(t) : t ∈ ℝ} implementing time evolution is strongly continuous: lim_(s → t)∥U(s)ψ − U(t)ψ∥ = 0 for every ψ ∈ ℋ.

A10^(′) is a strengthening of A10 specifically for the time-translation subgroup; strong continuity is the standard hypothesis required by Stone's theorem.

## Statement of the quantum-unitary theorem

:::
**Theorem 42** (Quantum-unitary evolution on the McGucken background). *Under Hypotheses A1--A11 and A10^(′), time evolution of quantum states on the separable complex Hilbert space ℋ is implemented by a unique strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group*
U : ℝ → 𝒰(ℋ),   U(t₁+t₂) = U(t₁)U(t₂),
*with self-adjoint infinitesimal generator Ĥ --- the Hamiltonian --- given by Stone's theorem:*
U(t) = e^(−iĤt/ℏ).
*The corresponding differential equation for any state ψ(t) = U(t)ψ(0) in the domain of Ĥ is the Schrödinger equation*
$$i\hbar\,\frac{d}{dt}\psi(t) \;=\; \hat{H}\,\psi(t).$$
*By the spectrum condition A11, the spectrum of Ĥ is bounded below; physical interpretation requires a unique ground state (vacuum).*
:::

The factor i in U(t) = e^(−iĤt/ℏ) is the standard Hermitian-generator convention: the infinitesimal unitary U(δt) = 𝟙 − iĤδt/ℏ + O(δt²) is unitary (to first order in δt) iff Ĥ is self-adjoint. This is the same i that appears in the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic --- the imaginary unit of ℂ --- but its appearance in the Schrödinger evolution is a consequence of unitarity, not a direct algebraic transport from the substrate law. The unification of "i in the substrate equation" with "i in unitary evolution" is the content of Novelty 2 of Section 1.

## Algebraic Channel: Algebraic derivation via Stone's theorem

Stone's theorem (Stone 1932, Reed--Simon I, Theorem VIII.8) states: *Every strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group {U(t) : t ∈ ℝ} on a Hilbert space ℋ has a unique self-adjoint infinitesimal generator Ĥ such that*
U(t) = e^(−iĤt/ℏ),
*and conversely, every self-adjoint operator Ĥ generates a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group via this exponential formula (defined via the functional calculus). The domain of Ĥ is the set of ψ ∈ ℋ for which the limit lim_(t → 0)(U(t)ψ−ψ)/t exists.*

Hypothesis A10^(′) supplies the strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group; Stone's theorem then directly produces the self-adjoint Ĥ and the Schrödinger equation. Uniqueness of Ĥ given U(t): if two self-adjoint operators Ĥ₁, Ĥ₂ both generate the same U(t), their difference annihilates every vector in a dense domain, hence equals zero by self-adjoint extension uniqueness.

Differentiation of U(t)ψ in t at t = 0 for ψ in the domain of Ĥ gives
$$\frac{d}{dt}U(t)\psi\Big|_{t=0} \;=\; -\frac{i}{\hbar}\hat{H}\psi,$$
which, applied to ψ(t) = U(t)ψ(0), gives the Schrödinger equation iℏ dψ/dt = Ĥψ. The differentiation is valid on the (dense) domain of Ĥ; on the rest of ℋ, the integrated form ψ(t) = U(t)ψ(0) remains valid.

## Geometric Channel: Geometric derivation via the Feynman propagator

The geometric content of quantum time evolution is the propagation kernel
K(x_(f),t_(f);x_(i),t_(i)) = ⟨x_(f)|U(t_(f)−t_(i))|x_(i)⟩,
which encodes the amplitude for a transition between configurations x_(i) at time t_(i) and x_(f) at time t_(f). The kernel satisfies the composition law
K(x_(f),t_(f);x_(i),t_(i)) = ∫K(x_(f),t_(f);x,t) K(x,t;x_(i),t_(i)) dx  for any  t_(i) < t < t_(f),
which is the geometric statement of the group law U(t_(f)−t_(i)) = U(t_(f)−t)U(t−t_(i)) for the unitary evolution.

Feynman's path-integral representation (1948) expresses the kernel as
K(x_(f),t_(f);x_(i),t_(i)) = ∫_(x(t_(i)) = x_(i))^(x(t_(f)) = x_(f))𝒟[x] e^(iS[x]/ℏ),
where the integral is over paths with the indicated endpoints and S[x] is the classical action. The factor i in e^(iS/ℏ) is again the Hermitian-generator convention applied to the path-action: the rigorous interpretation is via the Trotter product formula
U(t) = lim_(N → ∞)(e^(−iTt/(Nℏ)) e^(−iVt/(Nℏ)))^(N),
for a Hamiltonian of the form Ĥ = T + V (kinetic plus potential), whose continuum limit produces the formal e^(iS/ℏ) weighting; or alternatively via Wick rotation t →  − it to Euclidean signature and the Feynman--Kac representation, where the path measure becomes rigorously defined.

The geometric interpretation of the propagator on the McGucken background is: for a free relativistic particle of mass m, K is supported on (and inside, for massive particles) the future light cone of (x_(i),t_(i)), i.e., on the closure of the McGucken Sphere Σ⁺(x_(i),t_(i)). This is the *causality* content of the  + ic branch (A5): the propagation amplitude is non-zero only into the future of the initial event, reflecting the temporal orientation of the McGucken Principle.

## Channel-bridge synthesis

:::
**Proposition 43** (Channel synthesis for quantum-unitary evolution). *The Algebraic-Channel Stone generator Ĥ and the Geometric-Channel Feynman propagator K are equivalent representations of the same unitary evolution operator U(t): Ĥ is the infinitesimal generator obtained by Stone's theorem, and K is the integral-kernel representation of U(t) in the position basis. The bridge between them is the Trotter product formula (rigorous form) or the Feynman path-integral construction (formal form), with the shared invariant being the unitary group U(t) itself.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* By Stone's theorem, Ĥ uniquely determines U(t) = e^(−iĤt/ℏ). The integral kernel K(x_(f),t_(f);x_(i),t_(i)) = ⟨x_(f)|U(t_(f)−t_(i))|x_(i)⟩ is, by construction, the position-basis matrix element of the unitary operator U(t_(f)−t_(i)). Hence Ĥ and K are two representations of the same operator: the Hamiltonian description and the propagator description.

The Trotter product formula is the rigorous bridge. For Ĥ = T + V with T =  − ℏ²∇²/(2m) (kinetic) and V (potential), and under mild conditions on V ensuring that T + V is essentially self-adjoint on Schwartz functions, the formula
e^(−i(T+V)t/ℏ) = lim_(N → ∞)(e^(−iTt/(Nℏ)) e^(−iVt/(Nℏ)))^(N)
converges in the strong operator topology. The right-hand side, expanded in the position basis, gives a discretised sum over paths whose continuum limit is the Feynman path integral. Therefore the formal ∫𝒟[x]e^(iS/ℏ) representation is the limit of well-defined unitary products, and the Algebraic-Channel--Geometric-Channel equivalence is established rigorously via Trotter.

Alternatively, the Euclidean-signature path integral (Wick rotation t →  − iτ) defines a rigorous probability measure (the Wiener measure for the free Hamiltonian; the Feynman--Kac path-integral measure for Ĥ = T + V with V bounded below). The Minkowski-signature kernel is obtained by analytic continuation τ → it. This is the rigorous mathematical content of "the McGucken factor i in dx₄/dt = ic is the Wick rotation": the same i that converts Euclidean to Minkowski signature at the path-integral level is the i in the McGucken Principle, at the level of the substrate differential law. ◼
:::

# Discrete Symmetries: C, P, T, and the CPT Theorem
