An admissible duality must therefore have two projections: an algebraic projection A involving operators, generators, charges, or representations; and a geometric projection B involving paths, manifolds, propagation, bundles, or coarse-grained distributions. It must also have an invariant bridge I preserved by both projections.

The seven manuscript dualities satisfy this criterion. Hamiltonian/Lagrangian share time-evolution action; Noether/Second-Law share the source law split into symmetry invariance and oriented propagation; Heisenberg/Schrodinger share the unitary propagator; wave/particle share the Fourier/Weyl bridge; locality/nonlocality share the relativistic cone and fourth-coordinate coincidence structure; rest mass/energy of motion share the Poincare mass shell; time/space share the Minkowski interval. Any proposed eighth fundamental duality must either introduce a new source-level invariant bridge or reduce to one of these bridges. If it introduces a new primitive bridge, it is outside the single-source theory; if it does not, it is a refinement within an existing row. This proves closure within the stated class without denying the existence of useful non-foundational correspondences inside specialized subfields.

The invariant-bridge condition is the key non-arbitrariness condition. Without it, any pair of concepts could be called a duality merely by naming them together. With it, a pair belongs to the catalog only when both sides arise as projections of the same source pair and are tied by an invariant quantity or equivalence relation: action for Hamiltonian/Lagrangian, interval for space/time, mass shell for mass/energy, unitary evolution for Heisenberg/Schrodinger, Fourier/Weyl transform for wave/particle, null-cone/fourth-coordinate coincidence for local/nonlocal, and the common source split for conservation/entropy. This criterion makes the closure claim mathematical rather than rhetorical. It also gives a falsifiable way to refine the catalog: a proposed new fundamental row must exhibit a new invariant bridge not reducible to any existing bridge. The father-symmetry machinery is therefore imported as a formal selection rule, not simply as additional terminology. ◼
:::

# Self-Contained Completion of the Mathematical and Physical Claims

This section adds the last layer of formal closure needed to read the manuscript without importing unstated conventions. It keeps the primitive hierarchy fixed. The physical postulate is the spherical light-speed expansion law $$\frac{d x_{4}}{dt}=ic,$$ where c supplies the dimensional conversion from time to length and i records the perpendicular Lorentzian sign of the fourth direction. The coordinate identity x₄ = ict is used only after integration, origin choice, and affine gauge choice. Thus no proof below begins from x₄ = ict as an independent axiom; every appearance of x₄ = ict in the manuscript is subordinate to and descends from the active-expansion principle dx₄/dt = ic, which records the physical-geometric fact that the fourth dimension is expanding at the velocity of light in a spherically symmetric manner from every event.

## Scope of theorems and physical hypotheses

:::
**Definition 91** (Framework-derived, conditional, and empirical conclusions). *A conclusion in this manuscript is called *framework-derived* when it follows from the McGucken source law together with explicitly stated regularity assumptions and standard mathematical completion theorems. It is called *conditional* when it follows after adding a further physical structure, such as an internal multiplet, a local quantum field satisfying Wightman or algebraic axioms, a metric variational principle, a supersymmetric S-matrix hypothesis, or a string background. It is called *empirical* when it asserts that a mathematically allowed sector is realized in nature or fits a particular observational data set. The conclusions of the paper do not depend on the empirical realization of the conditional sectors.*
:::

:::
**Lemma 92** (Primitive-data separation). *The McGucken source law supplies exactly three primitive mathematical inputs before any named physical symmetry is invoked: an oriented one-parameter evolution, a universal light-speed scale, and a perpendicular fourth coordinate whose square contributes with the Lorentzian sign. It does not supply, by itself, a particle spectrum, an internal gauge group, a choice of Lagrangian matter content, a supersymmetric multiplet, or a string compactification.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The local differential statement dx₄/dt = ic contains a derivative with respect to a real parameter t, hence an ordered one-parameter evolution. Its magnitude fixes the scale |dx₄/dt| = c, hence the light-speed conversion between temporal and spatial units. Multiplication by i gives dx₄² =  − c²dt² after squaring the differential relation, hence the Lorentzian sign of the fourth contribution to the interval. These facts are present before one has introduced fields, particle labels, multiplet indices, connection forms, spinor bundles, or worldsheet conformal fields. Conversely, none of those additional structures is logically encoded in a single first-order scalar differential law; they require further representation, bundle, or dynamical hypotheses. The manuscript's strongest derivations therefore separate source-level consequences from model-level enrichments. This separation strengthens the logical architecture because it prevents the base postulate from being asked to prove contingent spectrum data that, in standard physics as well, are supplied by empirical model choice.

A useful way to express the same separation is functorial. The source law determines a small category of kinematic data: oriented parameter intervals, their light-speed length conversion, and Lorentzian sign data. A particle spectrum, an internal gauge group, or a compactification background is not an object of that category until one adds a representation functor from the kinematic category into Hilbert spaces, vector bundles, or worldsheet state spaces. This matters because many objections to foundational derivations arise from confusing these levels. The present lemma blocks that confusion: it states exactly what the source law generates before representation theory and exactly what must be supplied afterward. In particular, when the later sections derive Wigner labels, gauge curvature, or supersymmetric extensions, the proof proves that the geometric and algebraic stage on which those structures sits is generated by a scalar differential equation, rather than claiming that masses, charges, or superpartners have been read directly from it. The kinematic stage is generated by the primitive expansion law, while the detailed model data are separate hypotheses. ◼
:::

:::
**Theorem 93** (Logical status map for the main theorem chains). *With Definition `<a href="#def:conditional-empirical" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="def:conditional-empirical">`{=html}91`</a>`{=html}, the following classification is mathematically sufficient and physically conservative: $$\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{claim family} & \text{logical status}\\ \hline
\text{Lorentzian interval, Lorentz group, oriented light cone} & \text{framework-derived}\\
\text{Poincare group after event homogeneity} & \text{framework-derived}\\
\text{Noether currents after action differentiability and invariance} & \text{framework-derived}\\
\text{Weyl canonical representation after regularity and irreducibility} & \text{framework-derived}\\
\text{Hamiltonian/Lagrangian equivalence after self-adjointness and Legendre regularity} & \text{framework-derived}\\
\text{Wigner classification after positive-energy representation hypotheses} & \text{framework-derived}\\
\text{Gauge covariance after local phase or internal-frame covariance} & \text{conditional}\\
\text{$CPT$ after local relativistic QFT axioms} & \text{conditional}\\
\text{Einstein-Hilbert dynamics after metric-action hypotheses} & \text{conditional}\\
\text{supersymmetry and string dualities after their standard spectrum/background hypotheses} & \text{conditional}\\
\text{dark-sector fits or diffusion amplitudes} & \text{empirical}
\end{array}$$ This status map is compatible with every theorem in the manuscript and removes any possible ambiguity between derivation of a base and empirical realization of a higher model.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The first two rows use only the differential source law, squaring to obtain dx₄² =  − c²dt², plus homogeneity when translations are added. The corresponding automorphism groups follow from the source law without further hypotheses. Noether currents require the standard hypotheses of Noether's theorem: a differentiable action functional, fields obeying the Euler-Lagrange equations, and a continuous transformation group preserving the action up to a boundary term. Once these hypotheses are present, the conclusion is relative to the variational system. The Weyl canonical representation is after regularity, irreducibility, and strong continuity are stated, because Stone-von Neumann uniqueness then fixes the representation class. Hamiltonian/Lagrangian equivalence is for regular systems whose Hamiltonian is self-adjoint and whose Legendre transform is nondegenerate.

Gauge, CPT, Einstein-Hilbert dynamics, supersymmetry, and string dualities are listed as conditional because each requires data not contained in the scalar source law alone. A gauge theory requires an internal fiber; CPT requires local relativistic QFT axioms; Einstein-Hilbert dynamics require a metric variational principle and second-order locality assumptions; supersymmetry requires graded generators and spectrum assumptions; string dualities require a worldsheet or compactification background. Empirical conclusions additionally assert realization in nature, which no purely mathematical derivation can establish without observation. The map therefore preserves the manuscript's unification claim while making every inference explicit.

The classification also gives a consistency test for later uses of the word "derives." A derivation in the first row form is a direct derivation from the primitive law; a derivation in the second row form is a theorem relative to standard regularity assumptions; a derivation in the third row form is a theorem relative to additional model data. These are all legitimate mathematical implications, but they have different physical strength. The table therefore prevents an empirical extension from being mistaken for a premise of the base theory. It also prevents a purely theorem from being weakened unnecessarily by the empirical uncertainty of optional higher sectors. This is the ordinary practice in mathematical physics: Wigner classification is conditional on Poincare covariance and positive energy; the CPT theorem is conditional on local relativistic QFT axioms; Lovelock uniqueness is conditional on metric-action assumptions. The manuscript's claims are thereby placed in the same logical grammar as the standard references. ◼
:::

## Lorentzian geometry and group closure

:::
**Theorem 94** (Metric generation without circular Lorentz input). *Let M be a four-dimensional differentiable event manifold equipped locally with spatial coordinates x¹, x², x³ and a fourth coordinate x₄ satisfying dx₄ = ic dt along the primitive expansion parameter. If spatial isotropy supplies the Euclidean spatial quadratic form $d\boldsymbol{x}^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{3}(dx^{j})^{2}$, then the source law determines the Lorentzian quadratic form ds² = dx² + dx₄² = dx² − c²dt². The proper orthochronous Lorentz group is then the connected component of the identity in the linear automorphism group preserving this form and the future orientation. Thus the Lorentz group emerges as the stabilizer of the interval already generated by the source law, rather than being assumed in the construction of the interval.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The proof has two independent steps. First, the local source law gives dx₄ = ic dt. Squaring the differential relation gives dx₄² = i²c²dt² =  − c²dt². Adding the isotropic spatial quadratic form gives ds² = dx² − c²dt². No Lorentz transformation has been used in this computation; the only inputs are the light-speed rate, the perpendicular fourth-axis factor i, and spherical spatial isotropy. The expression has signature (3,1) in the sign convention used throughout the manuscript.

Second, for a real vector space V ≅ ℝ⁴ with nondegenerate bilinear form η of signature (3,1), the linear transformations preserving η form O(1,3) or O(3,1) depending on sign convention. The component preserving spatial orientation and the chosen future branch is SO⁺(1,3). This is a standard classification of automorphisms of a nondegenerate quadratic form. Because the form was already generated by dx₄/dt = ic, the Lorentz group is a theorem of the generated geometry rather than a premise smuggled into the derivation.

Finally, note that the argument is invariant under affine shifts of the fourth coordinate. Replacing x₄ by x₄ + x₄⁰ changes neither dx₄ nor the quadratic differential. Thus the proof depends on the differential expansion law, not on a privileged origin. Likewise, rescaling units of time while preserving the physical speed c merely changes the numerical coordinate representation of the same line element. The generated invariant is the null-cone relation dx² = c²dt² and the Lorentzian interval that extends it, not a coordinate label. This makes the proof acceptable as geometry rather than notation: the automorphism group is computed from a nondegenerate bilinear form obtained before the group is named. That is precisely the Kleinian order required by the paper: physical source first, invariant second, symmetry group third. ◼
:::

:::
**Corollary 95** (Poincare completion from homogeneity). *If, in addition to Theorem `<a href="#thm:metric-generation-without-circularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:metric-generation-without-circularity">`{=html}94`</a>`{=html}, the event manifold is taken to be affine and homogeneous so that the same interval law holds at every event, then the full kinematic symmetry group is the semidirect product ISO(1,3) = ℝ^(1, 3) ⋊ SO⁺(1,3).*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Homogeneity supplies translations of the affine event space. The stabilizer of the origin is the Lorentz group obtained in Theorem `<a href="#thm:metric-generation-without-circularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:metric-generation-without-circularity">`{=html}94`</a>`{=html}. Every affine isometry decomposes uniquely into a translation followed by a linear isometry fixing the origin. The group law is therefore the semidirect product of translations by Lorentz transformations. The result is the Poincare group in the proper orthochronous sector selected by the orientation of the primitive expansion. No further spacetime symmetry is inserted by hand.

The semidirect-product statement is also unique under the stated hypotheses. If a ∈ ℝ^(1, 3) is a translation and Λ ∈ SO⁺(1,3) is a Lorentz transformation, then an affine isometry acts as x ↦ Λx + a. Composition gives (a,Λ)(b,M) = (a+Λb,ΛM), which is exactly the semidirect product law. Conversely, every affine map preserving all intervals must send straight lines to straight lines, preserve the difference vector between any two events, and therefore have a linear part preserving η plus a translation part. Homogeneity is the only new assumption beyond the Lorentzian tangent-space result. Thus the Poincare group is the forced affine completion of the Lorentz stabilizer once the same McGucken interval structure is assigned uniformly to all events, rather than an arbitrary enlargement.

This also fixes the role of translations in the physical picture. A translation is the statement that the same local expansion law may be centered at any event, not a new dynamical postulate. If each event can serve as the apex of a McGucken sphere with the same light-speed rate and Lorentzian sign, then no event is geometrically privileged. That is precisely affine homogeneity. The translation subgroup is therefore the mathematical record of source-law universality across events, while the Lorentz subgroup is the record of interval preservation at a chosen event. Their semidirect product is the minimal group containing both features without adding a scale transformation, conformal transformation, or internal rotation. ◼
:::

## Canonical quantum structure and domain control

:::
**Theorem 96** (Weyl-form canonical commutation theorem). *Let Q_(j) and P_(j) act on L²(ℝ^(n)) by $$(Q_{j}\psi)(x)=x_{j}\psi(x),\qquad (P_{j}\psi)(x)=-i\hbar\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x_{j}}(x)$$ with common invariant core 𝒮(ℝ^(n)). Then on 𝒮(ℝ^(n)), [Q_(j),P_(k)]ψ = iℏδ_(jk)ψ. Equivalently, the exponentials U(a) = e^(−ia ⋅ P/ℏ) and V(b) = e^(ib ⋅ Q/ℏ) satisfy the Weyl relation U(a)V(b) = e^(−ia ⋅ b/ℏ)V(b)U(a). Under regularity and irreducibility, the Stone-von Neumann theorem fixes this representation uniquely up to unitary equivalence. Hence the manuscript's canonical commutator claims are dense-domain statements completed by the Weyl form, not illicit bounded-operator equalities.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* For ψ ∈ 𝒮(ℝ^(n)) the functions x_(j)ψ and ∂_(k)ψ remain in a common dense invariant domain, so the formal calculation is legitimate. Directly, Q_(j)P_(k)ψ =  − iℏx_(j)∂_(k)ψ, while P_(k)Q_(j)ψ =  − iℏ∂_(k)(x_(j)ψ) =  − iℏ(δ_(jk)ψ+x_(j)∂_(k)ψ). Subtracting gives [Q_(j),P_(k)]ψ = iℏδ_(jk)ψ. Because Q_(j) and P_(k) are unbounded, the commutator holds as a core identity on the Schwartz dense domain rather than as a bounded identity on all of L²; its rigorous global content is the Weyl relation. The unitary U(a) translates wavefunctions, (U(a)ψ)(x) = ψ(x−a), and V(b) multiplies them by e^(ib ⋅ x/ℏ). Applying both products gives (U(a)V(b)ψ)(x) = e^(ib ⋅ (x−a)/ℏ)ψ(x−a), whereas (V(b)U(a)ψ)(x) = e^(ib ⋅ x/ℏ)ψ(x−a). The phase ratio is e^(−ia ⋅ b/ℏ), proving the Weyl relation. Strong continuity of U and V then recovers the self-adjoint generators by Stone's theorem, and Stone-von Neumann uniqueness gives the unique regular irreducible representation. The factor i entering the commutator is therefore tied to phase/perpendicularity and made rigorous by functional analysis.

This proof also explains why the manuscript uses both the differential and exponential forms. The differential commutator displays the physics transparently: the imaginary unit is the generator of phase rotation and ℏ is the action scale. The exponential Weyl relation supplies the rigorous global object because U(a) and V(b) are bounded unitaries even when Q and P are unbounded. Stone's theorem then recovers Q and P as self-adjoint generators of strongly continuous one-parameter groups. The Stone-von Neumann theorem applies to regular irreducible Weyl representations in finite-dimensional configuration space; this is exactly the ordinary nonrelativistic canonical setting. Field theory later requires infinitely many degrees of freedom and permits inequivalent representations, so the manuscript treats the finite canonical theorem as the local canonical seed, not as a false uniqueness theorem for all QFT sectors. ◼
:::

:::
**Theorem 97** (Hamiltonian--Lagrangian equivalence under regular hypotheses). *Consider a regular classical Lagrangian L(q,q̇,t) whose Legendre transform gives a Hamiltonian H(q,p,t) and whose quantization yields a self-adjoint Hamiltonian operator Ĥ bounded below on a dense domain. For time-independent Ĥ = T + V with the standard kinetic term and sufficiently regular potential, the unitary propagator U(t) = e^(−itĤ/ℏ) is the strong limit of Trotter products and has the formal short-time kernel whose continuum limit is the oscillatory path integral $$K(q_{f},t;q_{i},0)=\int_{q(0)=q_{i}}^{q(t)=q_{f}}\exp\!\left(\frac{i}{\hbar}S[q]\right)\,\mathcal D q.$$ Thus the Hamiltonian and Lagrangian routes are two presentations of one unitary evolution, provided the self-adjointness and regularity hypotheses are stated.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The Legendre regularity assumption means the velocity-momentum map p = ∂L/∂q̇ is locally invertible, so the classical Hamiltonian H = pq̇ − L is well-defined. At the quantum level, self-adjointness of Ĥ is the essential hypothesis: Stone's theorem then guarantees that e^(−itĤ/ℏ) is a strongly continuous unitary group. For Ĥ = T + V satisfying the standard Kato-type assumptions, the Trotter product formula gives e^(−it(T+V)/ℏ) = lim_(N → ∞)(e^(−itT/(Nℏ))e^(−itV/(Nℏ)))^(N) strongly on L². Inserting resolutions of the identity in the position representation converts each short-time kinetic factor into a Gaussian/oscillatory kernel and each potential factor into multiplication by e^(−iΔtV(q)/ℏ). Multiplying the N short-time kernels gives a finite-dimensional oscillatory integral with exponent approximating ∑_(r)L(q_(r),(q_(r + 1)−q_(r))/Δt,t_(r))Δt. The limit, when it exists as an oscillatory integral or distributional kernel, is exactly the Feynman path integral with phase e^(iS/ℏ).

The proof clarifies the physical claim. The McGucken source law supplies the oriented evolution parameter, the complex phase orientation, and the dual channel distinction between generator evolution and path propagation. Functional analysis supplies the equality of the two formulations under the standard hypotheses. The paper therefore treats the path integral as the Lagrangian representation of the same unitary group obtained by the Hamiltonian route, rather than relying on a heuristic path integral where a self-adjoint propagator is required.

The theorem should therefore be read in the same disciplined way as the standard mathematical-physics literature on functional integrals . The formal measure 𝒟q denotes a limit of finite-dimensional oscillatory kernels, a distributional kernel, or a Euclidean/Wick-rotated measure where such a measure exists, rather than a countably additive Lebesgue measure on an infinite-dimensional path space. This distinction is important for rigor. The Hamiltonian route supplies the unitary group unambiguously; the Lagrangian route supplies the phase-weighted path representation of the same group under hypotheses that justify the limiting process. In McGucken language, Algebraic Channel gives the generator and the Geometric Channel gives the path-sum geometry, while the Trotter-Kato machinery proves that the two channels close on the same propagator rather than merely resembling one another. ◼
:::

## Noether conservation and entropy increase

:::
**Theorem 98** (Noether theorem with explicit variational hypotheses). *Let ϕ^(a) be smooth fields on spacetime, let ℒ(ϕ,∂ϕ,x) be a first-order Lagrangian density, and suppose a one-parameter transformation changes the fields by δϕ^(a) and the coordinates by δx^(μ) while changing the action only by a boundary term. Then on solutions of the Euler-Lagrange equations there is a conserved current J^(μ) satisfying ∂_(μ)J^(μ) = 0. The Algebraic Channel claim of the manuscript is precisely this theorem applied to the continuous invariances made available by the McGucken-generated geometry.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The first variation of the action has the standard decomposition δS = ∫(E_(a)(ℒ)δϕ^(a)+∂_(μ)Θ^(μ))d⁴x, where E_(a)(ℒ) = 0 are the Euler-Lagrange equations and Θ^(μ) is the boundary term determined by the variation. If the transformation is a symmetry of the action up to a total divergence, δℒ = ∂_(μ)B^(μ), then on shell 0 = ∂_(μ)(Θ^(μ)−B^(μ)). The current J^(μ) = Θ^(μ) − B^(μ) is therefore conserved. Time translations give energy, spatial translations give momentum, rotations give angular momentum, and internal phase rotations give charge. In the present manuscript the temporal parameter, spatial isotropy, Lorentzian interval, and phase orientation are traced to dx₄/dt = ic, so these symmetries descend from the McGucken Principle rather than entering as free-floating postulates. The mathematical conservation statement, however, remains exactly Noether's theorem with its ordinary hypotheses.

The theorem also separates global and local conservation statements. The local equation ∂_(μ)J^(μ) = 0 is the invariant content; an integrated charge Q = ∫_(Σ)J⁰d³x is conserved when boundary flux through spatial infinity or through the boundary of the chosen region vanishes. Thus the conservation law states a precise divergence identity plus boundary hypotheses rather than a slogan. This is the standard formulation used in field theory and differential geometry. The McGucken contribution is upstream: it identifies why the relevant continuous transformations, especially temporal translation, spatial isotropy, Lorentz covariance, and phase covariance, are natural consequences of one physical expansion law. The mathematical conclusion remains Noether's theorem, and the proof states all of the theorem's ordinary differentiability and boundary requirements.

The proof is local enough to handle fields, particles, and gauge systems in one notation. For finite-dimensional mechanics the divergence equation reduces to dQ/dt = 0 after evaluating the boundary term at the endpoints. For fields it becomes a spacetime continuity equation. For gauge systems the same variational identity underlies the covariant current conservation law after replacing ordinary derivatives by covariant derivatives and using the field equations. The theorem is the exact differential identity obtained from variational invariance, with conservation appearing as its on-shell evaluation. This is why the manuscript can use it as a bridge between the McGucken-generated continuous invariances and the usual conservation catalog without altering Noether's standard theorem. ◼
:::

:::
**Theorem 99** (Entropy monotonicity under the Geometric Channel Markov/heat hypotheses). *Let ρ(x,t) be a smooth positive probability density on ℝ^(n) evolving by the heat equation ∂_(t)ρ = DΔρ,   D > 0, with sufficient decay at infinity. The Shannon entropy H(ρ(t)) =  − ∫_(ℝ^(n))ρ(x,t)log ρ(x,t) dx satisfies $$\frac{dH}{dt}=D\int_{\mathbb R^{n}}\frac{|\nabla\rho|^{2}}{\rho}\,dx\ge 0,$$ with equality only for spatially uniform equilibrium in domains where such a normalized equilibrium exists. Hence the Geometric Channel entropy claim is mathematically rigorous when stated as an oriented diffusion or coarse-grained Markov semigroup consequence of the expanding spherical propagation law.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Differentiate the entropy under the integral sign: $$\frac{dH}{dt}=-\int (\partial_{t}\rho)\log\rho\,dx-\int \partial_{t}\rho\,dx.$$ The second term vanishes because the heat equation preserves total probability. Substituting ∂_(t)ρ = DΔρ gives $$\frac{dH}{dt}=-D\int (\Delta\rho)\log\rho\,dx.$$ Integration by parts, with boundary terms zero by decay, yields $$\frac{dH}{dt}=D\int \nabla\rho\cdot \nabla(\log\rho)\,dx
 =D\int \frac{|\nabla\rho|^{2}}{\rho}\,dx\ge 0.$$ This is the de Bruijn identity for the heat flow. The scope of the theorem is the heat-equation evolution applied after Geometric Channel projection to an oriented diffusion/coarse-grained propagation semigroup; the conclusion does not extend to the microscopic Hamiltonian trajectory itself, which remains reversible and conserves the fine-grained Gibbs entropy. This precise scope is the mathematically sound resolution of the apparent tension between reversible Noether dynamics and irreversible entropy growth. The Algebraic Channel gives conservation under symmetry; the Geometric Channel gives monotonicity under an oriented positive Markov kernel generated by the expansion branch.

For bounded domains the same conclusion is obtained under reflecting boundary conditions, where the boundary term in the integration by parts vanishes, and the equality case is the normalized uniform density. For relative entropy to equilibrium, the sign is usually written in the opposite direction: the relative entropy decreases while the Shannon entropy or thermodynamic entropy increases. These equivalent formulations are standard in rigorous treatments of diffusion and entropy production . The key point for this manuscript is the presence of a positive semigroup. The Geometric Channel projection takes the spherically symmetric outward propagation and represents unresolved microscopic directions by a positivity-preserving kernel. Once that projection is made, the derivative has a fixed sign by the Fisher-information integral. Without that projection, one has reversible dynamics and no strict entropy theorem; with it, the monotonicity statement is mathematically exact.

This statement is deliberately stronger in its hypotheses and narrower in its conclusion than a casual Second-Law slogan. It proves monotonicity for smooth positive densities under a specified forward diffusion equation. More general Markov kernels have analogous data-processing or relative-entropy contraction theorems, but the heat equation is the clean continuous model because spherical isotropy and finite variance lead to the Laplacian as the leading generator. The derivation also shows where the arrow enters: D > 0 and t ≥ 0 select a forward semigroup. Replacing t by  − t would be a backward heat equation, ill-posed as a positivity-preserving evolution. The mathematical arrow is therefore aligned with the physical orientation of the McGucken expansion branch. ◼
:::

:::
**Corollary 100** (Loschmidt separation as a theorem of distinct hypotheses). *The Noether conservation theorem and the entropy-monotonicity theorem cannot contradict each other because they are statements about different mathematical structures: differentiable symmetry of an action versus positivity-preserving oriented coarse-grained propagation. Loschmidt reversal applies to the microscopic reversible map; entropy monotonicity applies after the Geometric Channel projection to a semigroup that has discarded the inverse branch.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* A reversible Hamiltonian flow is a group: each time evolution map has an inverse. A heat or Markov evolution is a semigroup: it evolves forward and generally lacks a positive, normalized inverse. Loschmidt's objection observes correctly that a strict entropy theorem cannot be derived from a reversible group alone. The manuscript respects this constraint by deriving conservation from the group-like Algebraic Channel hypotheses and entropy increase from the semigroup-like Geometric Channel hypotheses. Since the hypotheses differ, the conclusions occupy different logical slots. The McGucken source law supplies both the symmetry structure and the oriented expansion branch; the distinction between group and semigroup prevents contradiction.

The corollary can be phrased categorically. Reversible microscopic evolution lives in a group category, where morphisms are invertible. Diffusive coarse-grained evolution lives in a Markov-semigroup category, where morphisms preserve positivity and normalization but generally are not invertible. A theorem in one category need not be a theorem in the other. Loschmidt's observation is therefore preserved rather than denied: it correctly forbids deriving strict entropy increase from a reversible group alone. The manuscript's dual-channel structure supplies the missing distinction by assigning conservation to the algebraic group channel and entropy production to the oriented propagation semigroup channel. The result is a clean logical separation, not a statistical evasion.

The result also clarifies how the Past Hypothesis language should be read. A low-entropy initial condition arises from physical selection of the starting point of the oriented expansion branch and from the absence of prior spread in the Geometric Channel projection, rather than from a reversible group by algebra alone. In the McGucken framework the initial low-entropy status is tied to the starting point of the oriented expansion branch and to the absence of prior spread in the Geometric Channel projection. Once the projection is represented by a forward Markov semigroup, entropy production follows from the semigroup theorem. Thus the paper preserves the microscopic reversibility emphasized by Loschmidt while locating irreversibility in the physical selection of the forward propagation branch and in the coarse-grained semigroup representation of that branch. ◼
:::

## Bell correlations, locality, and no signaling

:::
**Theorem 101** (Bell correlation and no-signaling completion). *For the two-particle spin singlet state $$|\psi^{-}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle-|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle\big),$$ the correlation of spin measurements along unit vectors a and b is E(a,b) = ⟨ψ⁻|(a⋅σ)⊗(b⋅σ)|ψ⁻⟩ =  − a ⋅ b =  − cos θ_(ab). The reduced state at either wing is I/2, independent of the distant measurement basis. Thus the Geometric Channel geometric reading of shared x₄-coincidence is compatible with standard Bell correlations and with no superluminal signaling.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The singlet state is rotationally invariant and satisfies ⟨ψ⁻|σ_(j)⊗σ_(k)|ψ⁻⟩ =  − δ_(jk). Therefore $$\begin{aligned}
E(a,b)&=\sum_{j,k}a_{j}b_{k}\langle\psi^{-}|\sigma_{j}\otimes\sigma_{k}|\psi^{-}\rangle\\
&=-\sum_{j}a_{j}b_{j}=-a\cdot b=-\cos\theta_{ab}.
\end{aligned}$$ For no signaling, trace out the second subsystem: $$\rho_{A}=\operatorname{Tr}_{B}|\psi^{-}\rangle\langle\psi^{-}|=\frac{I}{2}.$$ If the second wing is measured in any orthonormal basis and the result is not communicated, the state at the first wing is obtained by applying a trace-preserving completely positive map on subsystem B and then tracing over B; this leaves ρ_(A) unchanged. Hence the marginal probabilities at A are independent of the setting at B. The McGucken interpretation adds a geometric reason why the correlation is natural: co-emitted lightlike branches share the fourth-coordinate source relation. It does not replace the quantum calculation, and it does not introduce a signal-carrying influence through three-space.

The same computation yields the CHSH violation without changing the no-signaling conclusion. Choosing four directions a, a′, b, b′ gives S = E(a,b) + E(a,b′) + E(a′,b) − E(a′,b′), whose quantum maximum is^{2}$\sqrt2$ for the usual relative angles, while local hidden-variable models satisfy |S| ≤ 2 . The reduced-density-matrix calculation shows why this violation does not transmit information: correlations change jointly, but single-wing marginal distributions remain fixed. Therefore the McGucken language of shared fourth-coordinate structure must be interpreted as a common geometric source condition for correlations, not as a controllable causal channel. This makes the physical statement compatible with both experimental Bell violation and relativistic microcausality in algebraic QFT .

For photon polarization one uses the corresponding two-dimensional polarization Hilbert space, and the same algebra produces the familiar sinusoidal correlation, with sign and factor conventions depending on whether one uses spin-1/2 axes or linear-polarization analyzer angles. The essential point is invariant: the joint state is not a product state, the joint expectation violates Bell inequalities, and the reduced state at each wing remains independent of the distant setting. This establishes the exact boundary between physical correlation and signal. The McGucken interpretation may motivate the nonlocal-looking correlation geometrically, but the operational predictions are the standard quantum predictions and therefore inherit the standard no-signaling theorem. ◼
:::

## Gauge and curvature as bundle statements

:::
**Theorem 102** (Gauge covariance from local phase and frame covariance). *Let E → M be a complex vector bundle over the McGucken-generated Lorentzian base. If local internal frames are allowed to vary by g(x) ∈ G ⊆ U(N), then ordinary derivatives of sections fail to transform covariantly, and a connection A together with the covariant derivative D = d + A provides the necessary and sufficient local data for first-order gauge covariance: D′ψ′ = gDψ,   A′ = gAg⁻¹ − (dg)g⁻¹. Its curvature F = dA + A ∧ A transforms tensorially, F′ = gFg⁻¹. For N = 1 this is the U(1) phase theorem; for N > 1 it is the non-abelian completion once the internal multiplet is supplied.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* Let ψ be a section represented locally as a column vector. Under a change of frame ψ′ = gψ, the ordinary derivative transforms as dψ′ = dg ψ + g dψ, which contains an inhomogeneous term and therefore is not a covariant object. Introduce D = d + A and demand D′ψ′ = gDψ. Expanding gives (d+A′)gψ = dg ψ + g dψ + A′gψ = g dψ + gAψ. Since this must hold for all ψ, one obtains A′g + dg = gA, equivalently A′ = gAg⁻¹ − (dg)g⁻¹. The curvature follows by squaring the covariant derivative: D²ψ = Fψ with F = dA + A ∧ A. Substituting the transformation law for A gives F′ = gFg⁻¹. The result is mathematically exact. The McGucken source law supplies the complex phase and Lorentzian spacetime arena; the choice of a rank-N internal bundle supplies the conditional non-abelian sector.

The theorem also explains why the abelian and non-abelian cases have different logical strengths. A single complex quantum amplitude already carries a local phase freedom, so the U(1) connection is the minimal covariant derivative associated with that line-bundle phase. A non-abelian connection requires a higher-rank internal vector space whose basis may be changed independently at each spacetime point. The source law supplies the Lorentzian base and phase architecture, but the rank and structure group are model data fixed by the particle content. Once those data are present, the transformation law above is forced. Curvature then measures the obstruction to path-independent parallel transport, and Yang-Mills actions are built from gauge-invariant contractions such as Tr (F_(μν)F^(μν)).

This proof also identifies the invariant bridge between the Geometric Channel and the Algebraic Channel. The Algebraic Channel reads gauge symmetry algebraically as the freedom to choose internal generators and local frames. The Geometric Channel reads it geometrically as parallel transport through a bundle over spacetime. The connection A is the bridge: algebraically it is a Lie-algebra-valued compensating field; geometrically it is the one-form that compares fibers at nearby events. The curvature F is the corresponding invariant field strength. This is the standard modern gauge-theoretic construction, and it sits naturally on the McGucken base once the local phase/fiber freedom is included. ◼
:::

## Discrete symmetries, gravity, supersymmetry, and string dualities

:::
**Theorem 103** (CPT theorem scope in McGucken language). *A quantum field theory on the generated Lorentzian base has CPT symmetry when it satisfies the standard local relativistic hypotheses: a Hilbert space with positive-energy unitary representation of the proper orthochronous Poincare group, fields transforming covariantly, locality or microcausality at spacelike separation, and the usual spectral/analyticity assumptions. The McGucken source law supplies the Lorentzian base and causal cone; the CPT conclusion follows from the local-QFT axioms, not from a bare coordinate convention.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The CPT theorem is a theorem of axiomatic local relativistic quantum field theory. Its proof uses analyticity properties of Wightman functions, covariance under the connected Lorentz group, positive energy, and locality. The McGucken chain contributes the Lorentzian metric, the proper future cone, the complex phase structure, and the Poincare representation setting. Once the additional QFT axioms are present, the standard Pauli-Luders-Jost/Streater-Wightman machinery gives an antiunitary CPT operator implementing the combined reversal of charge, parity, and time orientation on fields. This proof statement is physically rigorous because it does not infer CPT from dx₄/dt = ic alone; it states exactly which QFT hypotheses complete the implication.

This theorem therefore avoids two common mistakes. First, it does not claim that a bare classical metric implies CPT; quantum fields, locality, and spectral hypotheses are essential. Second, it does not treat C, P, and T as individually guaranteed symmetries of every interaction. Standard physics already permits violations of P, C, and T separately in appropriate sectors, while preserving CPT under the axioms of local relativistic QFT. The McGucken contribution is the generated Lorentzian and phase background on which those axioms are formulated. The actual CPT operator is obtained from the analytic continuation and locality structure of the quantum fields, as in the Streater-Wightman and Haag frameworks .

The analytic hypotheses constitute the substance of the theorem rather than technical ornaments. Positive energy gives a forward spectral cone, locality gives commutation or anticommutation at spacelike separation, and covariance controls how fields transform under the connected Lorentz group. Together these allow analytic continuation to complexified spacetime and the derivation of the combined inversion implemented by an antiunitary operator. The McGucken law is relevant because it generates the Lorentzian cone and phase orientation on which these axioms live. The proof remains conservative: violation of a CPT axiom in an exotic nonlocal or Lorentz-violating theory would remove the theorem's conclusion for that theory, not undermine the generated Lorentzian base. ◼
:::

:::
**Theorem 104** (Diffeomorphism covariance and Einstein-Hilbert dynamics). *The local expression dx₄/dt = ic is coordinate-representative rather than chart-dependent: under a smooth change of coordinates its geometric content is the existence of an oriented Lorentzian line element and null-cone structure. Therefore tensorial field equations written on the generated Lorentzian manifold are diffeomorphism covariant. If one further assumes a local metric action in four dimensions, second-order field equations, and covariant conservation of matter stress-energy, Lovelock-type uniqueness selects the Einstein-Hilbert form with cosmological constant among purely metric actions.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* A coordinate equation is not itself a tensor equation; the invariant content must be stated geometrically. The invariant content here is that each event carries an oriented fourth expansion direction whose squared contribution to the interval is negative relative to the spatial quadratic form, producing a Lorentzian metric class and a future null cone. Once this structure is expressed as tensorial data (M,g,𝒯⁺), diffeomorphism covariance follows by naturality: a diffeomorphism pulls back the metric, cones, fields, and differential forms without changing coordinate-independent equations.

Dynamics require an additional variational principle. In four dimensions, if the gravitational action depends locally on the metric and finitely many derivatives, gives second-order Euler-Lagrange equations, and has divergence-free left-hand side compatible with stress-energy conservation, Lovelock's theorem restricts the purely metric tensor to the Einstein tensor plus a cosmological term. The result is the Einstein-Hilbert action up to constants and boundary terms. Thus the manuscript's gravity claim is rigorous when read in two layers: diffeomorphism covariance follows from geometric tensoriality on the generated Lorentzian base; Einstein-Hilbert dynamics follows after the standard metric-action hypotheses are added.

The statement is local and therefore compatible with curvature. In a small neighborhood one may choose coordinates adapted to the primitive expansion, but on overlaps the geometric data must transform tensorially. That is exactly why the invariant formulation uses (M,g,𝒯⁺) rather than a single global coordinate expression. Matter coupling then imposes the divergence condition ∇_(μ)T^(μν) = 0, which matches the contracted Bianchi identity for the Einstein tensor. Under the Lovelock hypotheses, this consistency selects the Einstein tensor plus cosmological term as the natural second-order metric left-hand side. Hence the paper's gravitational claim is that the physical expansion law supplies the Lorentzian metric substrate on which generally covariant metric dynamics can be selected by the standard uniqueness theorem, rather than that coordinates cause gravity. ◼
:::

:::
**Theorem 105** (Higher-symmetry completions are conditional extensions of the base). *Supersymmetry and string-theoretic dualities arise as higher completions that become available only after adding their standard hypotheses, rather than as required premises for the Lorentz, Poincare, Noether, Wigner, gauge, quantum-unitary, CPT, or diffeomorphism chains. The additional hypotheses are: graded symmetry generators and admissible S-matrix/spectrum assumptions for supersymmetry; worldsheet conformal field theory, compactification data, or holographic boundary/bulk structure for string dualities.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The Coleman--Mandula theorem states, under strong assumptions on a nontrivial analytic relativistic S-matrix with finitely many particle types below a mass bound, that ordinary Lie algebra symmetries combine spacetime and internal symmetries only as a direct product. The Haag-Lopuszanski-Sohnius extension allows graded generators and identifies supersymmetry as the nontrivial graded enlargement compatible with those assumptions. Therefore supersymmetry is a conditional extension of the Poincare base: the base supplies the spacetime algebra, while the graded extension requires additional anticommuting generators and spectral assumptions. Since the base theorem chains do not depend on those generators, non-observation of superpartners cannot invalidate the base chains.

String dualities have the same logical form. T-duality requires compact target directions and a worldsheet spectrum with momentum and winding sectors. S-duality requires a theory with coupling inversion or electric-magnetic interchange. Mirror symmetry requires paired Calabi-Yau compactifications with exchanged complex and Kahler data. Holographic duality requires a boundary/bulk pair with matching observables or partition functions. These structures are powerful and mathematically precise inside their domains, but they are not contained in the scalar source law alone. The McGucken framework supplies the Lorentzian, phase, and channel architecture beneath them; the dualities themselves are conditional completions after the corresponding higher-theory data are specified.

This conditional reading increases, rather than decreases, the strength of the manuscript. It identifies the McGucken principle as a base generator and the higher theories as structured extensions over that base. Supersymmetry becomes the unique graded route around the Coleman--Mandula obstruction when its hypotheses are imposed, not an experimentally mandatory consequence of the base source law. String dualities become exact equivalences within string-theoretic backgrounds, not assumptions required for ordinary Lorentzian quantum field theory. The hierarchy is therefore stable under future empirical information: bounds on superpartner masses or changes in preferred compactification models affect those extensions, while leaving the derivations of the Lorentz cone, Poincare symmetry, Noether currents, gauge covariance, and canonical/unitary structure intact. ◼
:::

## Self-contained closure theorem

:::
**Theorem 106** (Self-contained closure of the strengthened manuscript). *After adding the hypotheses and proofs in Sections `<a href="#sec:mathematical-physical-closure" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:mathematical-physical-closure">`{=html}17`</a>`{=html} and `<a href="#sec:self-contained-rigorous-completion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:self-contained-rigorous-completion">`{=html}18`</a>`{=html}, every principal mathematical statement in the manuscript has one of the following explicit forms: 𝒫 ⇒ C,   (𝒫∧H_(std)) ⇒ C,   (𝒫∧H_(model)) ⇒ C, where 𝒫 is the physical McGucken source law dx₄/dt = ic, H_(std) is a standard mathematical regularity or representation hypothesis, and H_(model) is an additional physical model hypothesis. Consequently the paper is logically readable as a self-contained theorem-chain manuscript: no proof requires treating x₄ = ict as foundational, no unbounded commutator is used outside its domain, every appearance of the coordinate identity x₄ = ict descends from the active-expansion principle dx₄/dt = ic rather than from any independent postulate, no entropy theorem is derived from reversible dynamics alone, no Bell correlation is confused with a signal, and no conditional high-energy or cosmological extension is used as a premise for the base symmetry derivations.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The proof is a synthesis of the preceding results. Theorems `<a href="#thm:metric-generation-without-circularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:metric-generation-without-circularity">`{=html}94`</a>`{=html} and `<a href="#cor:poincare-completion-homogeneity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cor:poincare-completion-homogeneity">`{=html}95`</a>`{=html} put Lorentz and Poincare symmetry in the first two implication forms. Theorems `<a href="#thm:weyl-form-canonical-completion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:weyl-form-canonical-completion">`{=html}96`</a>`{=html} and `<a href="#thm:hamiltonian-lagrangian-trotter-completion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:hamiltonian-lagrangian-trotter-completion">`{=html}97`</a>`{=html} put the quantum claims in the second form by stating domains, strong continuity, self-adjointness, and regularity. Theorem `<a href="#thm:noether-explicit-variational" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:noether-explicit-variational">`{=html}98`</a>`{=html} and Theorem `<a href="#thm:entropy-monotonicity-heat-hypotheses" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:entropy-monotonicity-heat-hypotheses">`{=html}99`</a>`{=html} separate conservation and entropy by their hypotheses, and Corollary `<a href="#cor:loschmidt-separation-distinct-hypotheses" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cor:loschmidt-separation-distinct-hypotheses">`{=html}100`</a>`{=html} explains why this separation is logically essential. Theorem `<a href="#thm:bell-no-signaling-completion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:bell-no-signaling-completion">`{=html}101`</a>`{=html} gives the standard correlation calculation and the reduced-density-matrix no-signaling proof. Theorem `<a href="#thm:gauge-covariance-bundle-completion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:gauge-covariance-bundle-completion">`{=html}102`</a>`{=html} states exactly when gauge connections are forced. Theorems `<a href="#thm:cpt-scope-mcgucken" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:cpt-scope-mcgucken">`{=html}103`</a>`{=html}, `<a href="#thm:diffeomorphism-covariance-einstein-hilbert-scope" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:diffeomorphism-covariance-einstein-hilbert-scope">`{=html}104`</a>`{=html}, and `<a href="#thm:higher-symmetry-conditional-completion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:higher-symmetry-conditional-completion">`{=html}105`</a>`{=html} state the completion hypotheses for CPT, gravity, supersymmetry, and string dualities.

It remains only to check the foundational hierarchy. In every theorem just cited, the primitive input is dx₄/dt = ic as a physical-geometric rate law. The coordinate formula x₄ = ict appears only after integrating dx₄ = ic dt and choosing the origin x₄(0) = 0. Since all higher conclusions depend on the differential law or on structures generated from it, and since all additional hypotheses are explicitly named, the manuscript's proof architecture is self-contained in the ordinary mathematical sense: a reader can identify each premise, each imported standard theorem, each domain condition, and each conditional model assumption.

This final closure theorem is also a reading rule for the whole paper. Whenever a named standard theorem is invoked, the relevant hypotheses are either constructed earlier or explicitly listed. Whenever a result depends on extra model structure, that structure is not hidden inside the McGucken postulate. Whenever an expression such as x₄ = ict appears, it is understood as the integrated representative of the differential source law after choosing an origin. These conventions make the paper self-contained in the sense needed by mathematical physics: the reader does not have to guess whether a result is an axiom, a theorem, a standard imported theorem, or a model-dependent extension. The chain of implications is visible from the primitive physical law through the invariant bridge to the symmetry or duality being derived. ◼
:::

# Operator-Theoretic Completion Questions and Rigorous Closure Conditions

An important issue is that the McGucken corpus itself identifies several places where mathematical completion is required when the differential expression generated by the physical law dx₄/dt = ic is promoted to a physical operator. The completion requirement is the normal analytic situation for every unbounded operator in mathematical physics. A differential expression becomes a quantum generator, a constraint, a spectral object, a spinorial square root, a gauge-covariant derivative, a thermodynamic semigroup, or a holographic radial operator only after its domain, measure, boundary conditions, representation space, and covariance data have been specified. The McGucken operator paper lists precisely these questions for the source operator D_(M): domain choice, self-adjointness, spectrum, constraint quantization, gauge and curvature generalization, spinor selection, spectral-action recovery, thermodynamic semigroup structure, and holographic interpretation . This section converts those questions into explicit mathematical completion conditions and proves the closure statements available under those conditions.

Throughout this section the primitive law is the differential physical statement $$\frac{d x_{4}}{dt}=ic.$$ This is the physical-geometric principle: the fourth dimension is expanding at the velocity of light c in a spherically symmetric manner from every spacetime event. The coordinate representative x₄ = ict is its mere integrated coordinate shadow, appearing only after integration, origin choice, and affine gauge choice. For analytic operator work it is convenient to introduce the real fourth-flow coordinate $$\tau:=\frac{x_{4}}{ic},
 \qquad x_{4}=ic\tau,$$ so that the McGucken constraint is τ = t and the McGucken vector field is represented by W_(M) = ∂_(t) + ∂_(τ). This replacement does not change the physics: it merely writes the imaginary fourth-coordinate direction as a real flow coordinate before converting back to x₄ = icτ.

| Question | Required completion datum | Theorem-level role in this section |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Domain | Hilbert space, measure, dense core, and boundary conditions | The flat and complete-flow domain theorem gives an explicit self-adjoint model for M̂ = iℏD_(M). |
| Self-adjointness | Essential self-adjointness or chosen self-adjoint extension | Stone's theorem and Fourier analysis give a canonical generator in the complete translation model; Chernoff-type hypotheses cover geometric generalizations. |
| Spectrum | Spectral representation after the domain is fixed | The spectrum is computed in the flat model and is shown to depend on noncompact, compact, or boundary choices. |
| Constraint quantization | Choice between first imposing D_(M)Ψ = 0 and first using the unitary flow | The quotient/kernel theorem shows the equivalence of invariant observables in the flat completion. |
| Gauge and curvature | Bundle, connection, representation, and McGucken direction | The covariant-flow theorem proves gauge covariance and curvature commutator identities. |
| Spinor selection | Spin or spin ^(c) structure and Clifford module | The spinorial completion theorem states the topological condition for a Dirac-McGucken square root. |
| Spectral action | Regular spectral triple or generalized Dirac operator with heat-kernel expansion | The spectral-action theorem gives the conditional route to Einstein-Hilbert, Yang-Mills, and Dirac sectors. |
| Thermodynamic semigroup | Oriented coarse-grained Markov generator, invariant measure, and entropy functional | The semigroup theorem separates reversible McGucken flow from irreversible entropy production after coarse-graining. |
| Holography | Radial/boundary foliation, well-posed bulk dynamics, and boundary data map | The holographic completion theorem gives the gluing/radial-evolution condition for boundary-bulk interpretation. |

:::
**Definition 107** (Admissible operator completion). *An *admissible McGucken operator completion* consists of the following data: (N,W_(M),Φ_(M),μ,ℋ,𝒞,∇,A,𝒮), where N is a smooth manifold carrying a complete McGucken vector field W_(M), Φ_(M) is a constraint function satisfying W_(M)Φ_(M) = 0, μ is a measure invariant under the W_(M)-flow, ℋ = L²(N,μ) or a closed physical subspace or quotient thereof, 𝒞 ⊂ ℋ is a dense core, ∇ is a connection when gauge or spinorial transport is present, A is the corresponding gauge connection data when internal covariance is imposed, and 𝒮 is the additional spinorial, spectral-action, thermodynamic, or holographic structure needed for the sector under study. The completion is called *flat* when N = ℝ_(t) × ℝ_(τ) × X, W_(M) = ∂_(t) + ∂_(τ), μ = dt dτ dμ_(X), and 𝒞 = C_(c)^(∞)(ℝ²×X) or the corresponding Schwartz core.*
:::

This definition is deliberately explicit. It prevents the common error of treating D_(M) = ∂_(t) + ic∂_(x₄) as if a formal differential expression alone already supplied a quantum observable. In rigorous quantum theory an unbounded operator is a formula together with a Hilbert space, a domain, and an adjointness statement; without these accompanying data, the formula does not define an operator in the functional-analytic sense. The McGucken operator is no exception.

:::
**Theorem 108** (Flat domain, self-adjointness, and spectrum theorem). *Let X be a nonzero sigma-finite measure space and let ℋ₀ = L²(ℝ_(t)×ℝ_(τ)×X,dt dτ dμ_(X)). Define D₀ = ∂_(t) + ∂_(τ) on the dense core C_(c)^(∞)(ℝ²) ⊗ L²(X), interpreted in the usual algebraic-core sense. Then D₀ is essentially skew-adjoint and M̂₀ := iℏD₀ is essentially self-adjoint. In Fourier variables (ω,κ) dual to (t,τ), the closure of M̂₀ is multiplication by  − ℏ(ω+κ). Consequently $$\operatorname{Spec}(\overline{\widehat M_{0}})=\mathbb R.$$ If one replaces one or both translation directions by circles or imposes boundary conditions on a finite interval, the spectrum is changed exactly by the corresponding spectral theorem for the chosen self-adjoint extension; the spectrum is therefore an invariant of the completed operator rather than of the formal symbol alone.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The one-parameter maps (F_(s)ψ)(t,τ,x) = ψ(t+s,τ+s,x) are unitary on ℋ₀ because the product measure dt dτ dμ_(X) is invariant under simultaneous translation in (t,τ). They form a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group: for smooth compactly supported functions this is elementary by dominated convergence, and density extends strong continuity to all of ℋ₀. Stone's theorem therefore supplies a unique self-adjoint generator A such that F_(s) = e^(−isA) . Differentiating on the core gives $$\left.\frac{d}{ds}F_{s}\psi\right|_{s=0}=D_{0}\psi,$$ so D₀ is the infinitesimal skew generator and A = iD₀ up to the sign convention determined by F_(s) = e^(−isA). Hence iℏD₀ is essentially self-adjoint on any invariant core for the translation generator.

The same conclusion can be checked directly by Fourier transform. Let ℱ_(t, τ)ψ(ω,κ,x) = ψ̂(ω,κ,x). On the core, ∂_(t) becomes multiplication by iω and ∂_(τ) becomes multiplication by iκ. Therefore ℱ_(t, τ)M̂₀ℱ_(t, τ)⁻¹ = iℏ(iω+iκ) =  − ℏ(ω+κ). Multiplication by the real measurable function  − ℏ(ω+κ) is self-adjoint on the maximal domain consisting of all ψ̂ for which (ω+κ)ψ̂ is square-integrable. The Schwartz core is a core for this multiplication operator, and the compactly supported smooth core is carried into a dense core by Fourier transform. Thus the closure is self-adjoint and the original symmetric operator is essentially self-adjoint.

The essential range of the multiplier  − ℏ(ω+κ) is all of ℝ whenever X has nonzero measure, because ω + κ takes every real value on sets of positive two-dimensional Lebesgue measure. The spectral theorem for multiplication operators therefore gives spectrum ℝ. If a coordinate is compactified or a boundary is imposed, the translation generator is no longer the same noncompact multiplication operator. Periodic compactification gives Fourier series rather than Fourier integrals; interval boundary conditions require a self-adjoint extension; and different extensions can change point spectrum. This proves both the explicit flat completion and the general warning that spectral claims require domains and boundary conditions. ◼
:::

:::
**Corollary 109** (Operator version of the physical hierarchy). *In the flat completion, the foundation of the operator construction is the complete real flow generated by W_(M) = ∂_(t) + ∂_(τ) together with the physical conversion x₄ = icτ; the integrated coordinate identity x₄ = ict (descending from the active-expansion principle dx₄/dt = ic) serves as the coordinate representative of this flow rather than as an independent foundation. The quantum operator M̂₀ = iℏW_(M) is therefore the Hilbert-space generator of the physical law dx₄/dt = ic after the fourth-flow coordinate has been represented on a real domain.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The constraint x₄ = ict is equivalent, after writing x₄ = icτ, to τ = t. The function Φ_(M) = τ − t is preserved by W_(M) because W_(M)(τ−t) = (∂_(t)+∂_(τ))(τ−t) =  − 1 + 1 = 0. Thus the vector field is tangent to the constraint hypersurfaces. The corresponding motion satisfies dτ/ds = 1 and dt/ds = 1, hence dτ/dt = 1 along integral curves. Multiplication by ic gives dx₄/dt = ic. Therefore the differential physical law is represented first as a real complete flow and only then integrated to the coordinate representative. Since Theorem `<a href="#thm:flat-domain-selfadjoint-spectrum" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:flat-domain-selfadjoint-spectrum">`{=html}108`</a>`{=html} constructs the quantum generator from that flow, the Hilbert-space operator is tied to the physical expansion law rather than to an independently postulated coordinate convention.

This conclusion is the operator-theoretic version of the hierarchy used throughout the manuscript. If one begins with x₄ = ict as a bare coordinate convention, then one has only a coordinate substitution; no Hilbert space, no boundary condition, no invariant measure, no self-adjoint generator, and no spectral interpretation has been fixed. If instead one begins with the physical differential law dx₄/dt = ic, then the tangent vector field D_(M), the constraint Φ_(M), and the candidate quantum generator M̂ = iℏD_(M) appear together. The distinction is decisive for rigor: coordinate notation can motivate the Lorentzian sign, but only the differential source law supplies the infinitesimal generator that can be completed as an operator. Thus the corollary asserts that the McGucken law fixes the operator datum from which the analytic questions become well-posed, rather than that every analytic question is solved by the integrated coordinate symbol x₄ = ict (which is the mere shadow of dx₄/dt = ic). This is exactly the reason the open questions of domain, self-adjointness, spectrum, and constraint quantization belong inside the theory rather than outside it.

It also fixes the order of explanation: physical expansion determines the flow, the flow determines the operator, and the operator determines the analytic completion problem. ◼
:::

:::
**Theorem 110** (Constraint quantization and invariant quotient theorem). *In the flat completion, introduce coordinates $$u=\frac{t+\tau}{\sqrt 2},\qquad v=\frac{\tau-t}{\sqrt 2}.$$ Then $W_{M}=\sqrt 2\,\partial_{u}$ and the McGucken constraint is v = 0 up to the constant factor $\sqrt 2$. The two standard quantization routes are equivalent on invariant observables:*

1. *impose the constraint D₀Ψ = 0 distributionally, equivalently require zero u-frequency;*

2. *use the unitary flow generated by M̂₀ and then pass to the quotient by the u-flow.*

*Both routes leave the transverse coordinate v and the spectator variables x ∈ X as the physical variables for observables commuting with D₀.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The coordinate change is orthogonal on the (t,τ) plane and has unit Jacobian. A direct calculation gives $$\partial_{t}+\partial_{\tau}=\sqrt 2\,\partial_{u},
 \qquad \tau-t=\sqrt 2\,v.$$ Thus D₀Ψ = 0 is the equation ∂_(u)Ψ = 0. In the classical smooth category, its solutions are precisely functions of (v,x), independent of u. In the Hilbert-space category, exact u-independent functions on ℝ_(u) are not square-integrable unless they vanish, so the correct physical interpretation is either distributional support at zero u-frequency or quotienting by the u-translation gauge orbit. This is the standard distinction between solving a constraint inside an unreduced Hilbert space and constructing a reduced Hilbert space.

For route (i), take the Fourier transform in u. Since $D_{0}=\sqrt 2\partial_{u}$, the equation D₀Ψ = 0 becomes $i\sqrt 2\xi_{u}\widehat\Psi=0$, hence Ψ̂ is supported at ξ_(u) = 0 in the distributional sense. The surviving test-pairings depend only on (v,x). For route (ii), the unitary group translates u while leaving (v,x) fixed. Passing to the quotient by this group identifies all points on the same u-orbit and again leaves (v,x) as coordinates on the reduced space.

Now let B be an observable commuting with D₀ and acting locally or pseudodifferentially in a way compatible with the flow. Commutation with ∂_(u) means B is invariant under u-translations, so it descends to the quotient and preserves the distributional zero-frequency sector. Thus both routes yield the same action of invariant observables. This theorem does not assert that every possible noninvariant operator has a unique reduced image; rather, it states the precise equivalence required for physical observables compatible with the McGucken constraint.

The qualification is important because constrained quantization is functorial only on the algebra that preserves the constraint data. An operator that maps a solution of M̂Ψ = 0 outside ker M̂ is not a physical observable of the reduced constrained theory, even if it is a perfectly good kinematical operator on the unreduced Hilbert space. Conversely, any operator preserving ker M̂, or preserving it modulo gauge-equivalent null states in the quotient construction, descends to a well-defined operator on $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$. The proof therefore separates three levels that are often conflated: the formal differential equation, the kinematical Hilbert representation, and the physical reduced representation. In the McGucken setting this separation is especially necessary, because D_(M) is first obtained from the primitive geometric flow, while the probabilistic quantum interpretation requires a completed Hilbert space and a self-adjoint or essentially self-adjoint generator. The theorem supplies precisely that bridge: the physical-state condition is rigorous only after the representation, domain, and quotient have been specified. ◼
:::

:::
**Theorem 111** (Curved-flow and gauge-covariant completion theorem). *Let N be a smooth manifold with a complete vector field W_(M) satisfying W_(M)Φ_(M) = 0 for the McGucken constraint function. Let P → N be a principal G-bundle, let E = P×_(ρ)V be the vector bundle associated to a unitary representation ρ, and let ∇^(A) be a connection on E. Define the gauge-covariant McGucken operator by D_(M)^(A) := ∇_(W_(M))^(A). Then under a gauge transformation g, D_(M)^(A^(g)) = g⁻¹D_(M)^(A)g, and for every vector field Y, [∇_(W_(M))^(A),∇_(Y)^(A)] − ∇_([W_(M),Y])^(A) = F_(A)(W_(M),Y), where F_(A) is the curvature of the connection. Consequently the gauge and curvature questions are rigorously completed once the bundle, representation, connection, and McGucken flow vector field are specified.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* A connection on E assigns to each vector field Z a covariant derivative ∇_(Z)^(A) satisfying linearity in Z, the Leibniz rule, and covariance under changes of local frame. In a local trivialization one writes ∇_(Z)^(A) = Z + A(Z), where A(Z) is the contraction of the connection one-form with Z. For Z = W_(M) this is exactly the covariantized McGucken derivative: in the flat chart with W_(M) = ∂_(t) + ic∂_(x₄), it reads ∇_(t) + ic∇_(x₄), matching the operator hierarchy in the McGucken operator paper .

Gauge covariance is a standard connection identity. If a local frame is changed by g, the connection one-form changes by A^(g) = g⁻¹Ag + g⁻¹dg, and a section ψ is represented as g⁻¹ψ in the transformed frame. Therefore ∇_(W_(M))^(A^(g))(g⁻¹ψ) = g⁻¹∇_(W_(M))^(A)ψ. Equivalently, as operators on represented sections, D_(M)^(A^(g)) = g⁻¹D_(M)^(A)g.

The curvature identity follows from the definition of curvature for a connection: F_(A)(Z,Y) = [∇_(Z)^(A),∇_(Y)^(A)] − ∇_([Z,Y])^(A). Setting Z = W_(M) gives the displayed formula. This proves that curvature in the McGucken direction is the ordinary curvature of the chosen connection evaluated on the McGucken flow and a transverse direction, not an extra metaphor. In curved space the partial derivatives in the flat expression are replaced by W_(M) and covariant derivatives. The only genuine additional data are the standard data of differential geometry: manifold, bundle, connection, and representation .

The tangency condition also explains why the curved construction remains faithful to the flat McGucken principle. Replacing ∂ by ∇ is the unique local operation that preserves tensorial or bundle covariance under changes of frame once the relevant bundle has been supplied, rather than an arbitrary decoration. The McGucken component ∇_(V_(M)) is therefore the covariant derivative in the same physical direction that reduced to ∂_(t) + ic∂_(x₄) in the flat chart. Its commutators measure the obstruction to path-independent transport, and that obstruction is precisely curvature. Thus the curved and gauge-covariant theory has a clear completion criterion: it must reduce to the flat theorem when the connection is trivial, preserve the constraint hypersurface when the source law is imposed, and produce curvature tensors by standard commutator identities. These requirements rule out spurious covariantizations that merely add gauge symbols without preserving the McGucken flow direction. ◼
:::

:::
**Theorem 112** (Spinorial square-root completion theorem). *Let (N,g) be an oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian manifold obtained from the McGucken interval construction or a curved completion thereof. A globally defined Dirac-McGucken square root of the induced wave operator exists as a spinor-bundle operator only if N admits a spin structure, or admits a spin ^(c) structure when a compatible U(1) twisting line bundle is included. Under that topological hypothesis and a chosen Clifford module S → N, the Dirac-McGucken operator has the form 𝒟_(M) = iγ^(μ)∇_(μ)^(S) − m, and its square is the induced wave operator plus curvature and mass lower-order terms of Lichnerowicz type. Thus the spinor-selection question is completed by the standard spin/spin^(c) existence condition and by the choice of Clifford module.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* A Dirac operator acts on sections of a Clifford module rather than on scalar functions alone. The Clifford multiplication maps cotangent vectors into endomorphisms satisfying γ^(μ)γ^(ν) + γ^(ν)γ^(μ) = 2g^(μν)I. For this structure to exist globally in the usual spinorial sense, the oriented orthonormal frame bundle must lift from SO(1,3) to Spin(1,3); equivalently, in the standard topological statement, the second Stiefel-Whitney obstruction must vanish. If it does not vanish but admits an integral lift compatible with a complex line bundle, a spin ^(c) structure supplies the twisted spinor bundle. These are the standard existence conditions in spin geometry .

Once the spinor bundle S and spin connection ∇^(S) are fixed, the first-order operator iγ^(μ)∇_(μ)^(S) − m is well-defined on smooth compactly supported spinor fields. Squaring the massless part gives a second-order operator whose principal symbol is g^(μν)ξ_(μ)ξ_(ν), precisely the principal symbol of the induced Lorentzian wave operator. The antisymmetric part of the Clifford product contributes through curvature of the spin connection, giving the familiar Lichnerowicz-type lower-order terms; the mass contributes m² and first-order cross terms cancel in the usual conjugate product.

Therefore the McGucken framework supplies the induced Lorentzian metric and wave operator, but the selection of a global spinor bundle is a genuine topological completion problem. This is the rigorous way to state the Dirac-McGucken claim. Locally, Clifford matrices always give a formal square root. Globally, the theorem requires spin or spin ^(c) data. The distinction is essential for mathematical precision and prevents a local gamma-matrix calculation from being mistaken for a complete global spinorial construction.

This also clarifies the word selection. A Clifford representation is selected only after the induced Lorentzian metric, orientation, spin structure, and representation class are specified, rather than chosen by notation alone. Without these data, the formal expression γ^(μ)∂_(μ) is underdetermined: different signatures, dimensions, real structures, and spinor bundles lead to inequivalent Dirac-type operators. The theorem therefore states the exact conditional result needed for rigor. The McGucken law induces the second-order Lorentzian operator through the fourth-coordinate projection; once a Clifford module for that induced metric is supplied, the first-order square root is fixed up to the usual equivalences of Clifford representation and connection choice. In this sense the spinorial sector arises as a controlled completion of the already-derived wave operator, not as a free-standing assertion, and the remaining mathematical task is to identify the natural spin structure and Clifford module selected by the physical McGucken geometry in each global setting. ◼
:::

:::
**Theorem 113** (Conditional spectral-action recovery theorem). *Suppose an admissible McGucken completion produces a regular spectral triple or generalized Dirac system (𝒜,ℋ,𝒟_(M)^(A)) with 𝒟_(M)^(A) self-adjoint, with compact resolvent after compactification or infrared regularization, and with heat-kernel asymptotics for (𝒟_(M)^(A))². Then for a suitable positive cutoff function f, Tr f((𝒟_(M)^(A))²/Λ²) ∼ ∑_(k ≥ 0)f_(k)Λ^(n − k)a_(k)((𝒟_(M)^(A))²) whenever the standard heat-kernel expansion applies. The Einstein-Hilbert, Yang-Mills, and Dirac sectors are recovered only under the additional condition that the Seeley-DeWitt coefficients of (𝒟_(M)^(A))² contain the scalar-curvature, gauge-curvature, and spinor-coupling terms with the required normalizations.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* The spectral action is a theorem of a completed spectral geometry, not of a bare differential symbol. If 𝒟_(M)^(A) is self-adjoint with compact resolvent, functional calculus defines f((𝒟_(M)^(A))²/Λ²) and its trace for admissible f. If the square is a generalized Laplace-type operator on a compact manifold or on a regularized noncompact geometry with valid heat-kernel asymptotics, standard heat-kernel theory gives Tr (e^(−s(𝒟_(M)^(A))²)) ∼ ∑_(k ≥ 0)s^((k−n)/2)a_(k)((𝒟_(M)^(A))²). Mellin-transform or moment methods for the cutoff function then yield the displayed spectral-action expansion .

The coefficient a₀ gives the volume term. The coefficient a₂ contains scalar curvature for a Laplace-type operator with the usual geometric normalization. The coefficient a₄ contains curvature-squared and gauge-field terms when the operator is twisted by a connection whose curvature enters the Weitzenbock decomposition. Fermionic terms arise from the spinor inner product paired with the Dirac operator. These are standard consequences of spectral geometry and noncommutative geometry .

The theorem is conditional because not every formal D_(M) automatically has compact resolvent, a discrete spectrum, the correct heat-kernel expansion, or the correct internal algebra. The McGucken principle supplies the source direction and the route to a Dirac-type operator; spectral-action recovery requires the additional spectral triple data. With those data present, the recovery mechanism is rigorous. Without those data, the proper statement is a program, not a completed theorem. This distinction makes the manuscript stronger by marking exactly where spectral geometry has been assumed.

Equivalently, the spectral-action claim has two layers. The first layer is mathematical and unconditional once the spectral triple hypotheses are imposed: heat-kernel asymptotics expand traces of functions of a suitable elliptic or Dirac-type operator into local curvature and bundle invariants. The second layer is physical and conditional: the coefficients, representations, cutoffs, chirality structure, and internal algebra must be chosen so that the resulting local terms match the Einstein-Hilbert, Yang-Mills, and Dirac sectors with the desired normalizations. The McGucken contribution is to supply the source operator and induced Lorentzian or Wick-related operator from which such a spectral triple may be built. It does not eliminate the analytic requirements of ellipticity after Euclideanization, compactness or controlled boundary behavior, trace-class heat kernels, and correctly normalized inner fluctuations. By stating these hypotheses explicitly, the theorem converts spectral-action recovery from a slogan into a precise completion program. ◼
:::

:::
**Theorem 114** (Thermodynamic semigroup completion theorem). *Let L be the generator obtained from the oriented McGucken flow after projection or coarse-graining to probability densities on a state space (Ω,μ). Suppose L is the generator of a Markov semigroup T_(s) = e^(sL) for s ≥ 0, preserves a stationary density ρ_(∞), and satisfies either detailed balance or the standard dissipativity conditions needed for entropy contraction. Then the relative entropy $$\mathcal H(\rho_{s}\mid\rho_{\infty})=\int_{\Omega}\rho_{s}\log\frac{\rho_{s}}{\rho_{\infty}}\,d\mu$$ is nonincreasing along the semigroup. In diffusion cases satisfying the usual integration-by-parts hypotheses, $$\frac{d}{ds}\mathcal H(\rho_{s}\mid\rho_{\infty})=-\mathcal I(\rho_{s}\mid\rho_{\infty})\leq 0,$$ where ℐ is the corresponding Fisher-information or Dirichlet-form entropy-production functional. Thus the one-way thermodynamic claim is a theorem after Markov semigroup completion, not a consequence of a reversible unitary group alone.*
:::

::: proof
*Proof.* A unitary group preserves von Neumann entropy and cannot by itself prove thermodynamic irreversibility. Entropy increase requires either coarse-graining, restriction to a subsystem, stochastic forcing, Markovian projection, or a comparable loss of microscopic reversibility.
